::: {.callout-note title="Sources"}
**CP-Algorithms**: Mo's algorithm (the block reordering, the $O(n\sqrt q)$ bound, the $B = n/\sqrt q$ block size), Mo's algorithm with updates, and "Mo's algorithm on trees" (cited here as the deferred variant) · **E-maxx / Hilbert-curve Mo ordering** (the space-filling-curve key) · **CLRS** ch. 17 (amortised bookkeeping for rollback) · **CPH** ch. 10 (the block idea shared with sqrt decomposition) · Sibling chapters: @sec-sqrt (blocks over positions and values — the *online* cousin) and @sec-seg (the fully general dynamic structure). Coverage: reordering range queries offline so a single window slides from one query to the next; the $n/\sqrt q$ block size and the $O(n\sqrt q)$ pointer-movement proof; rollback (append + snapshot/restore, no deletes); a third, time pointer for point updates at block size $n^{2/3}$; the Hilbert-order shortcut; and bolting a value structure (freq-of-freq, exact-$k$) onto the window.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- Recognise when a batch of *offline* range queries can be answered by sliding one window instead of building a structure — the tell is "no (or few) updates, and the answer changes in $O(1)$ when you add or drop one endpoint" (@sec-mo-a1).
- Sort queries into blocks of size $B = n/\sqrt q$ and prove the total two-pointer movement is $O(n\sqrt q)$ — and see *why* $n/\sqrt q$, not $\sqrt n$ (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1-powerful).
- Answer "how many distinct / equal-pairs / exact-$k$" style queries by maintaining an $O(1)$ `add`/`remove` pair over the window (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1-xorfav).
- Handle a structure with **append but no cheap delete** by rollback Mo: keep the right pointer monotone within each left-block, snapshot, add the $\le B$ left fringe, answer, restore (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2-interesting).
- Fold in point *updates* with a third (time) pointer at block size $n^{2/3}$, stashing the old value before overwriting it (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
- Replace block-sorting with the **Hilbert order** and measure the shorter walk it buys (@sec-mo-a4).
- Attach a value structure (a freq-of-freq table, an exact-$k$ counter) to the window so the answer is more than a single scalar (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5-threeocc).
- Triage Mo against segment tree, sqrt blocks, and persistent/Fenwick from the shape of the statement (@sec-mo-a6).
:::

## Why this matters {#sec-mo-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Suppose someone hands you $q$ range queries, $[l_1, r_1], \dots, [l_q, r_q]$, all up front, with **no updates in between**. A segment tree or a prefix table answers each on its own. Mo's algorithm does something stranger and often faster: it **reorders the queries** so that consecutive ones overlap heavily, then keeps a single window $[\ell, r]$ and *slides* it from one query to the next — expanding or shrinking one endpoint at a time. The trick works whenever you can maintain the answer cheaply as the window grows or shrinks by one cell: an `add(i)` that lets cell $i$ into the window and a `remove(i)` that kicks it out, each $O(1)$. Sort the $q$ queries by which block of size $B$ their $\ell$ lives in, and by $r$ inside the block, and the pointers travel only $O(n\sqrt q)$ steps in total. Because you shuffled the queries to make the walk short, you must remember each query's original index and print the answers back in that order — Mo is **offline**.
:::

Chapter @sec-sqrt put $\sqrt{n}$ blocks on *positions* and *values* to serve queries and updates **online**. This chapter is its offline sibling: instead of a structure you update, you keep one moving window and move it in the cheapest order through a whole batch of questions asked ahead of time. The payoff shows up when the batch is large, there are no (or very few) updates, and — crucially — the thing you are counting can be fixed or broken in $O(1)$ when a single cell enters or leaves the range. "Distinct values", "how many equal pairs", "is there a value appearing exactly once", "the XOR of every value seen an even number of times" — all of these slide.

Four statement shapes put you in Mo's territory:

| Statement hint | Why Mo fits / what rules others out | Which section uses it |
|---|---|---|
| "$q$ range queries, **all given up front**, no updates, $n, q \le 2\cdot10^{5}$" | Offline lets you reorder; $O(1)$ add/remove gives $O(n\sqrt q)$ | @sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1 |
| answer **appends** cheaply but **deleting** is hard / costs a rebuild | Rollback Mo: right pointer never moves left, snapshot + restore the fringe | @sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2 |
| queries are interleaved with **a handful of point updates** | Add a third, *time* pointer; block size $n^{2/3}$ | @sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3 |
| the raw window gives a scalar, but you need the **mode / exact-$k$ / a witness** | Bolt a freq-of-freq or bitmask table onto the window | @sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5 |

The whole chapter in one pipe: you are *given* every query, so you sort them to make the window's journey short, slide a single $[\ell,r]$ with $O(1)$ updates to the answer, and stash each result under the query's original id so the output is still in input order.

:::

The lessons build the toolkit in six steps:

- **A1 — The Mo core.** Offline reordering, block size $B = n/\sqrt q$, and the $O(n\sqrt q)$ pointer-movement proof (@sec-mo-a1).
- **A2 — Rollback Mo.** Append + snapshot/restore for structures with no cheap delete; monotone right pointer per left-block (@sec-mo-a2).
- **A3 — Mo with updates.** A third (time) pointer, block size $n^{2/3}$, and stashing the old value (@sec-mo-a3).
- **A4 — Hilbert order.** A space-filling-curve key that shortens the walk; measured against block-sort (@sec-mo-a4).
- **A5 — Mo plus a value structure.** freq-of-freq / exact-$k$ tables living inside the window (@sec-mo-a5).
- **A6 — Mo versus the rest.** Reading the statement to pick Mo, sqrt blocks, segment tree, or a persistent/Fenwick offline trick (@sec-mo-a6).

Part B turns the toolkit into five patterns, one per outline topic: classic Mo (@sec-mo-p1), rollback Mo (@sec-mo-p2), Mo with updates (@sec-mo-p3), Hilbert order (@sec-mo-p4), and Mo plus a value structure (@sec-mo-p5).

## Part A — Lessons

## A1. The Mo core: sliding one window {#sec-mo-a1}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
You have $q$ queries and an array of length $n$. Write a tiny state with two operations: `add(i)` (let cell $i$ into the current window) and `remove(i)` (kick it out), each $O(1)$, plus a running answer you update inside them. Hold the current window $[\ell, r]$ (inclusive) and, for each query, walk $\ell$ and $r$ from where they were for the previous query to the new one — each step is one `add` or `remove`. If you processed queries in *input* order the pointers could thrash $O(n)$ per query ($O(nq)$ total). Sorting by $\bigl(\lfloor \ell/B \rfloor,\ r\bigr)$ fixes that: inside one $\ell$-block, $r$ only ever moves forward (at most $n$ steps across the whole block) and $\ell$ moves at most $B$ steps per query. With $n/B$ blocks that is $O(n \cdot n/B)$ for $r$ and $O(q \cdot B)$ for $\ell$; total movement $O(n^2/B + qB)$, minimised when the two terms are equal, i.e. $B = n/\sqrt q$, giving $O(n\sqrt q)$.
:::

Here is the whole engine on the friendliest question — "how many **distinct** values are in $[l, r]$?" — with coordinate compression so the frequency table is small. Read the four `while` loops as the invariant "the window currently equals the last query's range":

```{python}
def mo_distinct(a, qs, B=None):
    """Answer 'count of distinct values in [l, r]' (0-indexed, inclusive) for every query by
    sliding one window in block order. Returns answers in the ORIGINAL query order."""
    n = len(a)
    if B is None:
        B = max(1, int(n / max(1, len(qs)) ** 0.5))    # the right default is n/sqrt(q), not sqrt(n)
    # coordinate-compress so freq[] is small even for huge values
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    distinct = 0
    cl, cr = 0, -1                     # current window is empty: [cl, cr] with cl > cr

    def add(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        freq[b[i]] += 1
        if freq[b[i]] == 1:            # this value just appeared for the first time in the window
            distinct += 1

    def remove(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        freq[b[i]] -= 1
        if freq[b[i]] == 0:            # this value just vanished from the window
            distinct -= 1

    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    ans = [0] * len(qs)
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        while cr < r:
            cr += 1; add(cr)
        while cl > l:
            cl -= 1; add(cl)
        while cl < l:
            remove(cl); cl += 1
        while cr > r:
            remove(cr); cr -= 1
        ans[i] = distinct              # stash under the query's original index
    return ans


a = [1, 3, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 3]
qs = [(0, 3), (1, 4), (2, 7), (0, 7)]
assert mo_distinct(a, qs) == [3, 4, 4, 4]     # {1,3,2}; {3,1,2,4}; {1,2,4,3}; {1,2,3,4}
```

The four moves look asymmetric, but they are the *only* order that keeps the window consistent — you always widen before you narrow so indices never go out from under you. Stress it against the one-line truth (`len(set(...))`) over random arrays, block sizes, and query sets:

```{python}
def distinct_brute(a, l, r):
    return len(set(a[l:r + 1]))


for _ in range(400):
    n = random.randint(1, 60)
    a = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 25)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    B = random.choice([1, max(1, int(n / q ** 0.5)), max(1, int(round(n ** 0.5))), n])
    got = mo_distinct(a, qs, B)
    exp = [distinct_brute(a, l, r) for l, r in qs]
    assert got == exp, (a, qs, B, got, exp)
```

One query's window $[\ell, r] = [1, 4]$ shaded green over a block size $B = 3$. Cell $0$ and cells $5..7$ sit outside and are *not* counted. The $\ell$-block boundary (a faint box around cells $3, 4, 5$) is what the sort groups by; $r$ sweeps left-to-right within it.

:::

Now the part beginners get wrong: **the block size is $n/\sqrt q$, not $\sqrt n$**. $\sqrt n$ is only optimal in the special case $q \approx n$. Price the actual pointer movement both ways on random query sets where $q \ll n$ and watch $n/\sqrt q$ win:

```{python}
def mo_move(qs, B):
    """Total |d_l| + |d_r| over the block-ordered walk — the real work Mo does."""
    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    move, prev = 0, (0, -1)
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        move += abs(l - prev[0]) + abs(r - prev[1])
        prev = (l, r)
    return move


rm = random.Random(7)
tot_good = tot_sqrt = 0
for _ in range(40):
    n = rm.choice([1000, 2000, 4000])
    q = rm.choice([100, 200, 400])                    # q much smaller than n
    qs = [tuple(sorted((rm.randrange(n), rm.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    tot_good += mo_move(qs, max(1, int(n / q ** 0.5)))   # B = n/sqrt(q)
    tot_sqrt += mo_move(qs, max(1, int(round(n ** 0.5))))  # B = sqrt(n)
assert tot_good < tot_sqrt                            # measured: the right block size is cheaper
```

::: {.callout-important title="The Mo core, in five lines"}
- Offline: sort queries by $\bigl(\lfloor \ell/B \rfloor, r\bigr)$ with $B = n/\sqrt q$.
- Maintain one window $[\ell, r]$ and an answer updated by `add`/`remove` in $O(1)$.
- For each query, walk the four pointers with the widen-then-narrow order shown above.
- Store the result in `ans[original_index]`; print in input order.
- Total movement $O(n^2/B + qB) = O(n\sqrt q)$. If you cannot write a $O(1)$ `remove`, you are in @sec-mo-a2 (rollback).
:::

## A2. Rollback Mo: append, snapshot, restore {#sec-mo-a2}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Some aggregates are easy to *build up* but painful to *undo*. Adding a cell to "number of equal pairs" is $O(1)$ (just add the current frequency), but there is no clean $O(1)$ `remove` that also retracts whatever `add` did to some other structure. Rollback Mo avoids deletes entirely: within a left-block, sort the queries by $r$ and move the right pointer **only forward** (never left, never a remove). Keep the "clean" part of the window as $[\text{blockEnd}+1, R]$. For each query, snapshot, temporarily `add` the short *left fringe* $\ell \dots \text{blockEnd}$ (at most $B$ cells), read the answer, then **restore** the snapshot. Because the fringe is tiny and gets rolled back every query, and $R$ never retreats, total work is still $O(n\sqrt n)$ — with not a single delete.
:::

The canonical add-only aggregate is **the number of equal pairs in $[\ell, r]$** (this exact cost is what CF 868F minimises). `add(i)` bumps the pair count by the frequency the value already had; a stack of `(value, old_freq)` lets `rollback` pop the fringe away in $O(B)$ and reset the pair count to the snapshot.

```{python}
def rollback_pairs(a, qs, B=None):
    """Number of unordered equal pairs in [l, r] (inclusive), answered by rollback Mo (no deletes)."""
    n = len(a)
    if B is None:
        B = max(1, int(round(n ** 0.5)))
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    pairs = 0
    hist = []                          # (value, freq_before) for every add, so we can undo

    def add(i):
        nonlocal pairs
        v = b[i]
        hist.append((v, freq[v]))
        pairs += freq[v]               # this new cell pairs with each earlier copy already inside
        freq[v] += 1

    def snapshot():
        return len(hist), pairs

    def rollback(snap):
        nonlocal pairs
        hh, pp = snap
        while len(hist) > hh:
            v, old = hist.pop()
            freq[v] = old
        pairs = pp

    def pairs_in(l, r):                # brute for a query that lives wholly inside one block
        c = Counter(a[l:r + 1])
        return sum(x * (x - 1) // 2 for x in c.values())

    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    ans = [0] * len(qs)
    last_block, R = -1, -1
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        bl = l // B
        block_end = min(n - 1, (bl + 1) * B - 1)
        if bl != last_block:           # start a fresh left-block: drop the whole window
            rollback((0, 0))
            R = block_end
            last_block = bl
        while R < r:                   # right pointer only ever advances — never a remove
            R += 1
            add(R)
        if r <= block_end:             # short query, entirely inside the block: brute it
            ans[i] = pairs_in(l, r)
            continue
        snap = snapshot()
        for j in range(block_end, l - 1, -1):    # temporarily add the left fringe, at most B cells
            add(j)
        ans[i] = pairs
        rollback(snap)                          # undo the fringe; the clean [blockEnd+1, R] survives
    return ans


a = [1, 2, 1, 1, 3, 2, 1]
qs = [(0, 6), (1, 3), (0, 2), (4, 6)]
# [0,6]: 1x4 ->6 pairs, 2x2 ->1, total 7 ; [1,3]=[2,1,1] ->1 ; [0,2]=[1,2,1] ->1 ; [4,6]=[3,2,1] ->0
assert rollback_pairs(a, qs) == [7, 1, 1, 0]
```

The `snapshot` is just a stack height and the pair total — $O(1)$ — and `rollback` only pops the at-most-$B$ fringe cells, so the amortisation is honest. Verify against a brute pair-counter:

```{python}
for _ in range(400):
    n = random.randint(1, 60)
    a = [random.randint(0, 4) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 25)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    B = max(1, int(round(n ** 0.5)))
    got = rollback_pairs(a, qs, B)
    exp = [sum(x * (x - 1) // 2 for x in Counter(a[l:r + 1]).values()) for l, r in qs]
    assert got == exp, (a, qs, got, exp)
```

rb_B = 3

def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, rb_a, x=0.0, y=1.6,
            regions=[(0, rb_B, "green", "left fringe $\\leq B$ (added, then rolled back)"),

Within one left-block, the window splits into a **fringe** (the $\le B$ cells from $\ell$ to the block end, added fresh and rolled back every query) and a **clean tail** $[\text{blockEnd}+1, R]$ that $R$ only ever extends rightward. No cell is ever removed from the tail — that is the whole point of rollback.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="When to reach for rollback instead of classic Mo"}
Use rollback when `remove` is expensive or impossible but `add` is cheap: e.g. maintaining a sorted/DSU structure, a stack of "last occurrence" links, or a value that only combines. The cost is the same $O(n\sqrt n)$, but you must be able to **snapshot and restore both the scalar answer and the auxiliary table** (here `pairs` *and* `freq` via `hist`) — restoring only the number and leaving the table dirty is the classic rollback bug (@sec-mo-pit).
:::


## A3. Mo with updates: a third, time pointer {#sec-mo-a3}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Now updates *do* appear, but few — say the input is "interleave $q$ range queries and $m$ point updates". Give the window a third pointer: besides $[\ell, r]$ you track `t`, *how many* of the updates have been applied. Moving `t` forward applies the next update and moving it back reverts the last one — for that you must have **saved the cell's old value before overwriting it**, or you cannot undo. Now a query has a triple $(\ell, r, t)$ and you sort by $\bigl(\lfloor \ell/B \rfloor, \lfloor r/B \rfloor, t\bigr)$. The right block size is no longer $n/\sqrt q$ but $B = n^{2/3}$: with three pointers the movement splits into three terms — $\ell$-jitter $O(qB)$, $r$-sweeps $O(n^2/B)$, and $t$-sweeps $O(m\,n^2/B^2)$ — and for $m \sim n$ the $\ell$ and $t$ terms balance at $B = n^{2/3}$, giving $O(n^{5/3})$.
:::

Keep "count distinct" and add updates `(pos, x)` that set `a[pos] = x`. Applying an update when `pos` is inside the window must first `remove` the old value's contribution and then `add` the new one; when `pos` is outside, you just change the stored value so it reads correctly if the window later slides over it.

```{python}
def mo_with_updates(a0, queries, updates):
    """queries: (l, r, t) with t = number of the FIRST updates already applied (inclusive window).
    updates: list of (pos, newval). Returns count-of-distinct in [l, r] after the first t updates."""
    a = list(a0)
    n = len(a)
    comp = {}

    def id_of(v):
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        return comp[v]

    b = [id_of(v) for v in a]
    for pos, x in updates:
        id_of(x)                       # make sure every update value has an id too
    freq = [0] * (len(comp) + 1)
    distinct = 0
    cl, cr, ct = 0, -1, 0              # window [cl, cr] with ct updates applied

    def add(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        freq[b[i]] += 1
        if freq[b[i]] == 1:
            distinct += 1

    def remove(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        freq[b[i]] -= 1
        if freq[b[i]] == 0:
            distinct -= 1

    ups = [[pos, x, None] for pos, x in updates]   # third slot: the stashed OLD value

    def apply_time():                  # move ct forward by one
        nonlocal ct, distinct
        pos, x = ups[ct][0], ups[ct][1]
        ups[ct][2] = a[pos]            # STASH the old value before overwriting — else no undo
        nid = id_of(x)
        if cl <= pos <= cr:            # only disturb the window if the changed cell is inside it
            freq[b[pos]] -= 1
            if freq[b[pos]] == 0:
                distinct -= 1
            freq[nid] += 1
            if freq[nid] == 1:
                distinct += 1
        a[pos] = x
        b[pos] = nid
        ct += 1

    def revert_time():                 # move ct back by one, using the stash
        nonlocal ct, distinct
        ct -= 1
        pos, x, old = ups[ct]
        nid = b[pos]
        oid = id_of(old)
        if cl <= pos <= cr:
            freq[nid] -= 1
            if freq[nid] == 0:
                distinct -= 1
            freq[oid] += 1
            if freq[oid] == 1:
                distinct += 1
        a[pos] = old
        b[pos] = oid

    B = max(1, int(round(n ** (2 / 3))))
    order = sorted(range(len(queries)),
                   key=lambda i: (queries[i][0] // B, queries[i][1] // B, queries[i][2]))
    ans = [0] * len(queries)
    for i in order:
        l, r, t = queries[i]
        while cr < r:
            cr += 1; add(cr)
        while cl > l:
            cl -= 1; add(cl)
        while cl < l:
            remove(cl); cl += 1
        while cr > r:
            remove(cr); cr -= 1
        while ct < t:
            apply_time()
        while ct > t:
            revert_time()
        ans[i] = distinct
    return ans


a0 = [1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]
ups = [(1, 1), (3, 4)]                 # 1-indexed in the raw idea; here 0-indexed for the demo
# queries as (l, r, t): after t updates applied
qs = [(0, 5, 0), (0, 5, 1), (0, 7, 2)]
# t=0: [1,2,3,1,1,2] distinct {1,2,3}=3 ; t=1 (a[1]=1): [1,1,3,1,1,2] {1,3,2}=3 ;
# t=2 (a[3]=4): [1,1,3,4,1,2,2,2] whole [0,7] {1,3,4,2}=4
assert mo_with_updates(a0, qs, ups) == [3, 3, 4]
```

The stash is the whole difficulty. Stress against naive replay — for each query, copy the array, apply the first `t` updates, and count distinct by hand:

```{python}
def distinct_replay(a0, updates, l, r, t):
    arr = list(a0)
    for k in range(t):
        pos, x = updates[k]
        arr[pos] = x
    return len(set(arr[l:r + 1]))


for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 40)
    a = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(n)]
    u = random.randint(0, 15)
    updates = [(random.randrange(n), random.randint(0, 5)) for _ in range(u)]
    q = random.randint(1, 15)
    queries = [(*sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n))), random.randint(0, u))
               for _ in range(q)]
    got = mo_with_updates(a, queries, updates)
    exp = [distinct_replay(a, updates, l, r, t) for l, r, t in queries]
    assert got == exp, (a, updates, queries, got, exp)
```

::: {#fig-mo-updates}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.flow(ax, p, {
        "l": (-3.2, 1.3, "move $\\ell$  $O(1)$", "green"),
        "r": (3.2, 1.3, "move $r$  $O(1)$", "green"),
        "t": (0.0, -0.4, "move $t$: apply/revert\none update (needs stash)", "pink"),
        "sort": (0.0, -2.3, "sort by\n$(\\lfloor \\ell/B \\rfloor, \\lfloor r/B \\rfloor, t)$", "indigo"),
    }, [("l", "t", ""), ("r", "t", ""), ("t", "sort", "$B = n^{2/3}$")], w=3.1, h=0.9)
V.show(draw)
```

Three pointers, one sort key. The time axis $t$ is what distinguishes Mo-with-updates: each $t$-step is an `apply_time`/`revert_time`, and the old value *must* be stashed on the way in so the way out is possible.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="The $n^{2/3}$ is not a magic tweak"}
With only $\ell, r$ the per-query $\ell$-jitter was $O(B)$ while $r$ swept $O(n)$ per block. Add $t$: the sort keys on $(\lfloor\ell/B\rfloor,\ \lfloor r/B\rfloor,\ t)$, so within each of the $(n/B)^2$ $(\ell,r)$-cells the $t$-pointer advances monotonically $O(m)$ times — a $t$-movement of $O(m\,n^2/B^2)$. The full cost is therefore three terms, $O(qB) + O(n^2/B) + O(m\,n^2/B^2)$ ($\ell$-jitter, $r$-sweeps, $t$-sweeps). With $m \sim n$ the $\ell$ and $t$ terms are equalised when $B^3 = n^2$, i.e. $B = n^{2/3}$, and both come out $O(n^{5/3})$ while the $r$ term $O(n^{4/3})$ is dominated. Using $B = \sqrt n$ instead leaves the $t$ term at $O(mn)$ — $O(n^2)$ once $m \sim n$, measurably worse — and the top CF solutions all size $B$ by $n^{2/3}$ (@sec-mo-p3-ml).
:::

## A4. Hilbert order: a shorter walk, same engine {#sec-mo-a4}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Block-sorting is a crude way to make consecutive queries *near* each other in $(\ell, r)$ space. A **Hilbert curve** is a single line that folds the 2D grid of $(\ell, r)$ points so that points close along the curve are also close in the plane. Compute each query's position on that curve — an integer key `hilbertOrder(l, r)` — and sort by it. You lose the tidy $O(n\sqrt q)$ proof (Hilbert gives the same asymptotic bound with a better constant), but in practice the pointers travel measurably fewer steps, and the code is just a different sort key over the same `add`/`remove` window.
:::

The recursive key below is the standard one (per cp-algorithms / kactl). Feed it to any Mo engine in place of the block key:

```{python}
def hilbert_order(x, y, pow=21, rot=0):
    """Position of (x, y) on the Hilbert curve of side 2^pow. Returns an integer sort key."""
    if pow == 0:
        return 0
    hpow = 1 << (pow - 1)
    if x < hpow:
        seg = 0 if y < hpow else 3
    else:
        seg = 1 if y < hpow else 2
    seg = (seg + rot) % 4
    rotate_delta = [3, 0, 0, 1]
    nx, ny = x % hpow, y % hpow
    nrot = (rot + rotate_delta[seg]) % 4
    sub = 1 << (2 * pow - 2)
    ans = seg * sub
    add = hilbert_order(nx, ny, pow - 1, nrot)
    ans += add if seg == 1 or seg == 3 else (sub - add - 1)
    return ans
```

The engine is A1's classic window with one line changed — the sort key. Keep the movement counter from A1 so the two orderings can be compared on the *same* random queries:

```{python}
def mo_distinct_ordered(a, qs, keyfn, count_move=False):
    n = len(a)
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    distinct = 0
    move = 0
    cl, cr = 0, -1
    prev = (0, -1)

    def add(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        freq[b[i]] += 1
        if freq[b[i]] == 1:
            distinct += 1

    def remove(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        freq[b[i]] -= 1
        if freq[b[i]] == 0:
            distinct -= 1

    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: keyfn(qs[i]))
    ans = [0] * len(qs)
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        if count_move:
            move += abs(l - prev[0]) + abs(r - prev[1])
        prev = (l, r)
        while cr < r:
            cr += 1; add(cr)
        while cl > l:
            cl -= 1; add(cl)
        while cl < l:
            remove(cl); cl += 1
        while cr > r:
            remove(cr); cr -= 1
        ans[i] = distinct
    return (ans, move) if count_move else ans
```

Correctness first — Hilbert changes the *order*, never the answer:

```{python}
def hilb_key(q):
    return hilbert_order(q[0], q[1])


def blk_key(q, B):
    return (q[0] // B, q[1])


for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 60)
    a = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 25)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    exp = [distinct_brute(a, l, r) for l, r in qs]
    assert mo_distinct_ordered(a, qs, hilb_key) == exp
print("Hilbert-ordered Mo is correct")
```

Now the measured payoff. On the *same* random query sets, count the total pointer steps for block-sort versus Hilbert and confirm Hilbert is the shorter walk:

```{python}
tot_h = tot_b = 0
rm = random.Random(12345)
for _ in range(40):
    n = rm.choice([800, 2000, 4000])
    qs = [tuple(sorted((rm.randrange(n), rm.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(n)]
    B = max(1, int(n / n ** 0.5))
    tot_b += mo_distinct_ordered([0] * n, qs, lambda q: blk_key(q, B), count_move=True)[1]
    tot_h += mo_distinct_ordered([0] * n, qs, hilb_key, count_move=True)[1]
assert tot_h < tot_b                   # Hilbert moves the window strictly less here
```

::: {#fig-mo-hilbert}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
hb_block, hb_hilbert = tot_b, tot_h
hb_best = min(hb_block, hb_hilbert)
hb_scaled = [round(hb_block / hb_best * 100), round(hb_hilbert / hb_best * 100)]

def draw(ax, p):
    V.bars(ax, p, hb_scaled, x=0.0, y=0.0,
           colors={0: "muted", 1: "green"}, labels=True)
V.show(draw)
```

Total pointer movement, normalised to the smaller (Hilbert) = 100: block-sort (grey) versus Hilbert order (green) summed over the measured trials. Hilbert trades a slightly uglier key for a genuinely shorter walk — which is why top-ranked Mo solutions reach for it when $n, q$ are large.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="Getting the key right"}
`pow` must satisfy $2^{\text{pow}} > \max(n)$ (the side length covers the grid); `pow=21` clears $2\cdot10^6$. Use a 64-bit integer in C++ ($4^{\text{pow}}$ overflows `int`), and rotate consistently — a wrong `rotate_delta` still produces a permutation, just a *longer* path, so tests pass while the constant silently worsens (@sec-mo-pit).
:::


## A5. Mo plus a value structure: when the answer is more than a number {#sec-mo-a5}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A lot of Mo problems are not "how many distinct" but something about the *shape* of the frequencies inside the range: the **mode** (largest frequency), "how many values appear **exactly** $k$ times", "is there a value appearing exactly once" (CF 1000F), "does every value appear at least / at most $t$ times" (CF 1418G). The window already keeps `freq[v]`. Add a **second table** that is also updated in $O(1)$ on every `add`/`remove`: `ftf[f]` = how many values currently have frequency exactly `f`. Then the mode is "the largest `f` with `ftf[f] > 0`" and "count of values appearing exactly $k$ times" is just `ftf[k]`. Keeping two tables consistent — and updating *both* in lockstep — is the entire extra difficulty.
:::

```{python}
def mo_exact_k(a, qs, k, B=None):
    """Count values that appear EXACTLY k times in [l, r] (inclusive), for each query."""
    n = len(a)
    if B is None:
        B = max(1, int(n / max(1, len(qs)) ** 0.5))
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    ftf = [0] * (n + 5)                 # ftf[f] = number of values whose current frequency is f
    cl, cr = 0, -1

    def add(i):
        v = b[i]
        old = freq[v]
        if old > 0:
            ftf[old] -= 1               # v is leaving frequency 'old'
        freq[v] = old + 1
        ftf[old + 1] += 1               # and entering frequency 'old+1'

    def remove(i):
        v = b[i]
        old = freq[v]
        ftf[old] -= 1
        freq[v] = old - 1
        if old - 1 > 0:
            ftf[old - 1] += 1

    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    ans = [0] * len(qs)
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        while cr < r:
            cr += 1; add(cr)
        while cl > l:
            cl -= 1; add(cl)
        while cl < l:
            remove(cl); cl += 1
        while cr > r:
            remove(cr); cr -= 1
        ans[i] = ftf[k]
    return ans


a = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]
qs = [(0, 6), (3, 5), (0, 2)]
# [0,6]: freqs 1->1,2->2,3->3,4->1 ; exactly-once values {1,4}=2
# [3,5]=[3,3,3] -> exactly-once 0 ; [0,2]=[1,2,2] -> exactly-once {1}=1
assert mo_exact_k(a, qs, k=1) == [2, 0, 1]
```

The two tables must move together — a `add`/`remove` that edits `freq` but forgets `ftf` is the most common bug in this family. Stress against a `Counter` oracle, and also drive the **mode** (largest frequency) from the same table to show the reuse:

```{python}
def exact_k_brute(a, l, r, k):
    return sum(1 for x in Counter(a[l:r + 1]).values() if x == k)


for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 60)
    a = [random.randint(0, 4) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 25)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    B = max(1, int(n / q ** 0.5))
    for k in (1, 2, 3):
        got = mo_exact_k(a, qs, k, B)
        exp = [exact_k_brute(a, l, r, k) for l, r in qs]
        assert got == exp, (k, a, qs, got, exp)
print("exact-k value-structure stress OK")
```

::: {#fig-mo-ftf}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
ftf_win = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]          # a window with freqs v=1->1, v=2->2, v=3->3

def draw(ax, p):
    V.array(ax, p, ftf_win, x=0.0, y=2.2,
            colors={i: "green" for i in range(len(ftf_win))},
            regions=[(0, 6, "muted", "the window")], label="a[window]")
    V.grid(ax, p, [["value", "v=1", "v=2", "v=3"],
                   ["freq[v]", "1", "2", "3"],
                   ["ftf[f]#", "1", "1", "1"]],
           x=0.0, y=0.2, colors={(1, 1): "indigo", (1, 2): "indigo", (1, 3): "indigo"}, cell_w=1.2)
V.show(draw)
```

The window $[1,2,2,3,3,3]$ keeps `freq[v]` per value **and** `ftf[f]` = how many values sit at frequency $f$ (here one value each at $1, 2, 3$). "Exactly one value with frequency $2$" reads straight off `ftf[2] = 1`; the mode reads off the largest index with `ftf > 0`.

:::

::: {.callout-important title="What can ride on the window"}
Anything you can maintain in $O(1)$ per `add`/`remove`: freq-of-freq arrays (mode, exact-$k$, "all counts $\le t$"), a set of "currently-present" values (CF 1000F's single-occurrence witness), or a single "how many values are off-target" counter (the exactly-thrice decision of @sec-mo-p5-threeocc). The Mo skeleton is unchanged — only the payload grows. Beware the look-alikes: CF 1000F genuinely lives in this family (@sec-mo-p4-oneocc), but CF 1418G counts good *subarrays* (a two-pointer / hashing sweep) and CF 985F's isomorphism is a *positional* bijection no frequency table can express — both are cited, never solved as Mo, in @sec-mo-p5.
:::

## A6. Mo versus the rest: a triage {#sec-mo-a6}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Mo is one of several tools for "many range queries". Pick it by reading the statement, not by habit. **Segment tree / Fenwick** win when queries must be answered *online* (the next query depends on your previous answer) or when updates interleave heavily — Mo cannot reorder them. **Sqrt decomposition** (@sec-sqrt) is the online, easy-to-code middle ground with $O(\sqrt n)$ per op and *no reordering*. **Mo** is the offline specialist: many queries, few/no updates, and a $O(1)$ slide. **Persistent / offline-BIT tricks** fit when the query is really "prefix up to $r$ with a static rule" (k-th number, count $< x$). The single tell for Mo: you may answer the queries in *any* order and get to keep one moving window.
:::

::: {#fig-mo-triage}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.flow(ax, p, {
        "q": (0.0, 2.6, "many range\nqueries?", "muted"),
        "online": (-3.6, 0.4, "must answer\nonline / depends\non last answer?", "pink"),
        "upd": (3.6, 0.4, "few or no\nupdates?", "green"),
        "slide": (0.0, -1.8, "answer moves in\n$O(1)$ per add/remove?", "indigo"),
        "mo": (-3.2, -3.6, "Mo's algorithm\n(this chapter)", "green"),
        "seg": (3.4, -3.6, "segment tree /\nFenwick / sqrt", "muted"),
    }, [("q", "online", "yes"), ("q", "upd", ""), ("online", "seg", "yes"),
        ("upd", "slide", ""), ("slide", "mo", "yes"), ("slide", "seg", "no")], w=2.6, h=1.1)
V.show(draw)
```

The decision tree. Reordering freedom is the gate: if you can permute the queries (offline, few updates) and the answer slides in $O(1)$, Mo is your tool. If either fails, @sec-sqrt's blocks or @sec-seg's tree is the honest answer — and forcing Mo onto adaptive input is a wrong-algorithm bug, not a slow one.

:::

Cross-reference: @sec-sqrt-a6 drew the *other* side of this boundary — "sqrt versus Mo versus segment tree" from the block-decomposition point of view. The two triages are the same fork seen from opposite doors: sqrt decomposition keeps the queries in input order and pays $O(\sqrt n)$ online; Mo spends the reordering freedom to slide one window and pays $O(n\sqrt q)$ offline.

## Part B — Patterns

Each pattern below is one *way of moving the window* — how the queries are ordered, what the `add`/`remove` maintain, and what extra pointer or table the statement forces on you. The two solved problems per pattern put that shape on a real (or fully-stressed, self-authored) task and check the sliding answer against a brute force.

**Where we are.** The five patterns climb one idea at a time on top of A1's core. Pattern 1 is the bare engine — a $O(1)$ `add`/`remove` and block order (@sec-mo-p1). Pattern 2 removes the `remove`: when only `add` is cheap, rollback keeps the right pointer monotone (@sec-mo-p2). Pattern 3 adds a third, *time* pointer so a few interleaved updates can be applied and reverted (@sec-mo-p3). Pattern 4 keeps two pointers but orders them by a Hilbert curve instead of by blocks, trading a tidy proof for a shorter walk (@sec-mo-p4). Pattern 5 keeps the plain window but hangs a whole *value structure* off it, because the answer is no longer one scalar (@sec-mo-p5). Pattern 1 is the toolkit; 2–5 are what it buys once the statement gets harder.

## P1. Classic Mo: order, slide, restore {#sec-mo-p1}

**The engine in the wild.** @sec-mo-a1's window — sort by block-of-$\ell$ then $r$, keep an $O(1)$ `add`/`remove`, stash answers by original id — is the whole solution the moment a problem's answer moves by a constant amount per cell. The two problems below differ only in *what* the $O(1)$ update maintains: a squared-count scalar (CF 86D) and a pair count over a prefix-xor table (CF 617E).

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Sort, then slide one $[\ell, r]$.** Order queries by $\bigl(\lfloor \ell/B \rfloor, r\bigr)$ with $B = n/\sqrt q$; the four widen-then-narrow loops move only to the next query (@sec-mo-a1).
- **The answer must update in $O(1)$ per add/remove.** CF 86D adds $(2f+1)v$; CF 617E adds `freq[p ^ k]`. Find the *one-line* delta, and Mo applies.
- **If you cannot write a cheap `remove`, this is the wrong pattern** — jump to @sec-mo-p2 (rollback).
- **Offline discipline.** Reordering shuffles the queries; write `ans[id]` and print in input order (@sec-mo-pit).
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-86d-powerful-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a squared-count to a pair count.** The previous problem kept one scalar and updated it by $(2f+1)v$. The next keeps a *frequency-of-prefix-xor* table and counts how many window pairs xor to $k$ — same window, but the answer lives over *pairs*, and the query range shifts by one into prefix-index space.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-617e-xor-and-favorite-number/problem.qmd >}}



## P2. Rollback Mo: append, snapshot, restore {#sec-mo-p2}

**When `remove` is the enemy.** @sec-mo-a2's rule: if the aggregate can be *extended* in $O(1)$ but a symmetric `remove` is awkward or you simply do not want to write one, do not delete at all. Group the queries by their $\ell$-block, and inside a group sweep the right pointer **only forward**; per query, snapshot, add the small left fringe, read, and roll the fringe back. The two problems below are the same engine wearing two payloads: CF 703D maintains an XOR-over-even-counts toggle, and a self-authored range-distinct task maintains a plain distinct counter. (A note on the roster: CF 703D also admits a trivial classic-Mo `remove`; it is solved in rollback form here to exercise the pattern end-to-end. The judge problem where rollback is genuinely the standard solution is CF 868F, cited below.)

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Monotone right pointer per left-block.** Sort queries by $(\lfloor \ell/B \rfloor, r)$; $R$ only advances within a group, so it is never a delete (@sec-mo-a2).
- **Snapshot = a stack height plus the scalar answer.** `add` pushes the one `freq` cell it dirties; `rollback` pops back to the height and restores the scalar — restoring *only* the scalar and leaving the table dirty is the classic bug (@sec-mo-pit).
- **The left fringe is $\le B$ cells.** Add it, read the answer, roll it back; the clean tail $[\text{blockEnd}+1, R]$ survives untouched.
- **Short (same-block) queries are brute-forced.** There is no tail to reuse, so scan the $\le B$ cells directly.
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-703d-mishka-and-interesting-sum/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a parity toggle to a plain counter.** The previous problem's `add` flipped membership of a value with an XOR. The next keeps the same monotone-$R$, snapshot-fringe skeleton but maintains the simplest possible payload — "how many distinct values are in the range" — to show rollback is a *window discipline*, not a specific formula.]{.flow-bridge}

### Problem: Distinct values per range, by rollback {#sec-mo-p2-distinct}

::: {.p-statement}
*Self-authored (no judge link).* An array $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le n \le 2\cdot 10^{5}$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^{9}$) and $m$ queries $[\ell, r]$. For each query output the number of **distinct** values in $a_\ell, \ldots, a_r$.

Example — $a = [1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3]$: $[1,7]$ has $\{1,2,3\}$, answer `3`; $[1,3] = [1,2,1]$ has $\{1,2\}$, answer `2`; $[4,6] = [3,3,2]$ has $\{3,2\}$, answer `2`. (Checked against a `set` oracle on the example, then stressed.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Distinct-count is the canonical $\sqrt n$-friendly window: `add(i)` raises `freq[v]` from $0$ to $1$ and increments a `distinct` counter only on that $0 \to 1$ edge, everything else in $O(1)$. We answer it **in rollback form on purpose** — never calling `remove`, only `add` on a monotone right pointer plus a temporary fringe that is snapshotted and restored. The point is to prove the pattern is payload-agnostic: whatever `add` does, `snapshot` just records the stack height and the running counter, and `rollback` unwinds both.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Set size.** Per query, $\lvert \operatorname{set}(a[\ell..r]) \rvert$ in $O(r - \ell + 1)$ — the oracle.
2. **Rollback Mo.** Block by $\ell$, monotone $R$ per group, snapshot $(\mathit{hist}, \mathit{distinct})$, add the fringe, read, roll back; same-block queries use the set oracle.

**Invariant.** After advancing $R$ to $r$ the clean tail $[\text{blockEnd}+1, R]$ holds a `freq`/`distinct` consistent with those cells; the fringe adds for $[\ell, \text{blockEnd}]` bump `distinct` on each first appearance; reading after the fringe gives the true count over $[\ell, r]$, and restoring the snapshot returns the tail to its pre-fringe state.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Count a set per query

::: {.form-next}
For each query return $\lvert \operatorname{set}(a[\ell..r]) \rvert$ in $O(r - \ell + 1)$ — reference only.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def dc_brute(a, l, r):
    return len(set(a[l:r + 1]))


assert [dc_brute([1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3], l, r) for l, r in [(0, 6), (0, 2), (3, 5)]] == [3, 2, 2]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: number of distinct values in one range via a set
int dc_brute(const vector<long long>& a, int l, int r) {
    set<long long> s;
    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) s.insert(a[i]);
    return (int)s.size();
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** 0-indexed inclusive here, 1-indexed on the (authored) input; the example subtracts one.

#### Rollback Mo (never call `remove`)

::: {.form-next}
Monotone right pointer per left-block; `add(i)` bumps `distinct` only when `freq[v]` leaves $0$; snapshot the stack height and `distinct`, add the $\le B$ fringe, read, restore. Same-block queries fall back to the set count. $O(n\sqrt n)$, zero deletes.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: sec-mo-p2-distinct-sol
def distinct_rollback(a, qs, B=None):
    """qs are (l, r) 0-indexed inclusive; count distinct values, answered by rollback Mo (no deletes)."""
    n = len(a)
    if B is None:
        B = max(1, int(round(n ** 0.5)))
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    distinct = 0
    hist = []

    def add(i):
        nonlocal distinct
        v = b[i]
        hist.append((v, freq[v]))
        if freq[v] == 0:                 # first appearance in the window
            distinct += 1
        freq[v] += 1

    def snapshot():
        return len(hist), distinct

    def rollback(snap):
        nonlocal distinct
        hh, dd = snap
        while len(hist) > hh:
            v, old = hist.pop()
            freq[v] = old
        distinct = dd

    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    ans = [0] * len(qs)
    last_block, R = -1, -1
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        bl = l // B
        block_end = min(n - 1, (bl + 1) * B - 1)
        if bl != last_block:
            rollback((0, 0))
            R = block_end
            last_block = bl
        while R < r:
            R += 1
            add(R)
        if r <= block_end:
            ans[i] = dc_brute(a, l, r)
            continue
        snap = snapshot()
        for j in range(block_end, l - 1, -1):
            add(j)
        ans[i] = distinct
        rollback(snap)
    return ans


assert distinct_rollback([1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3], [(0, 6), (0, 2), (3, 5)]) == [3, 2, 2]
for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 50)
    a = [random.randint(0, 7) for _ in range(n)]
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(15)]
    assert distinct_rollback(a, qs, max(1, int(round(n ** 0.5)))) == [dc_brute(a, l, r) for l, r in qs]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// rollback Mo for distinct-count (full program); right pointer never retreats, fringe is snapshotted
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<long long> raw(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> raw[i];
    map<long long, int> comp;
    vector<int> b(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (!comp.count(raw[i])) comp[raw[i]] = (int)comp.size();
        b[i] = comp[raw[i]];
    }
    int m; cin >> m;
    int B = max(1, (int)sqrt((double)n));
    vector<array<int, 3> > qs(m);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int l, r; cin >> l >> r; --l; --r;
        qs[i] = {l, r, i};
    }
    sort(qs.begin(), qs.end(), [B](const array<int,3>& x, const array<int,3>& y) {
        if (x[0] / B != y[0] / B) return x[0] / B < y[0] / B;
        return x[1] < y[1];
    });
    vector<int> freq(comp.size(), 0);
    vector<long long> ans(m, 0);
    vector<pair<int, int> > hist;
    int distinct = 0;
    auto add = [&](int i) {
        int v = b[i];
        hist.push_back(make_pair(v, freq[v]));
        if (freq[v] == 0) distinct++;
        freq[v]++;
    };
    auto rollback_to = [&](int hh) {
        while ((int)hist.size() > hh) {
            int v = hist.back().first;
            freq[v] = hist.back().second;
            hist.pop_back();
        }
    };
    int last = -1, R = -1;
    for (int qi = 0; qi < m; ++qi) {
        int l = qs[qi][0], r = qs[qi][1], id = qs[qi][2];
        int bl = l / B;
        int be = min(n - 1, (bl + 1) * B - 1);
        if (bl != last) { rollback_to(0); distinct = 0; R = be; last = bl; }
        while (R < r) { R++; add(R); }
        if (r <= be) {
            set<int> s;
            for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) s.insert(b[i]);
            ans[id] = (int)s.size();
            continue;
        }
        int hh = (int)hist.size(); int d0 = distinct;
        for (int j = be; j >= l; --j) add(j);
        ans[id] = distinct;
        rollback_to(hh); distinct = d0;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) cout << ans[i] << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `add` touches exactly one `freq` cell and possibly `distinct`, and records that cell's previous value in `hist`; `rollback_to(hh)` rewinds `hist` and then resets `distinct` to the snapshot — the same "restore the table *and* the scalar" discipline as CF 703D. The window is over compressed ids, so `freq` is sized to the number of distinct values, not to $10^{9}$.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Set per query:** $O(n)$, $O(nm)$ reference only. **Rollback Mo:** $O(n\sqrt n)$ $O(1)$ adds with $B = \sqrt n$, space $O(n)$ — the same envelope as @sec-mo-a1 but built without a single `remove`.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Query inside one block: `distinct` is read from a fresh set scan, never from the (empty) tail.
- All-equal array: every add after the first leaves `distinct` unchanged; the $0\to1$ guard is the whole correctness.
- Large values ($10^{9}$): compressed to ids for `freq`, so the frequency table stays $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 703D · Mishka and Interesting sum](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/703/D){rating="2100"} — the same rollback skeleton with a parity-toggle payload (@sec-mo-p2-interesting)
- [CF 220B · Little Elephant and Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/220/B){rating="1800"} — a distinct-flavoured window solved with a value-axis split instead (@sec-sqrt-p4-learray)
:::

## P3. Mo with updates: a third, time pointer {#sec-mo-p3}

**When updates sneak in.** @sec-mo-a3's extension: the input mixes range *queries* with a handful of point *updates*, but the whole batch is still offline, so you may reorder it. Give the window a third pointer `t` = how many updates have been applied, read each query as a triple $(\ell, r, t)$, and sort by $\bigl(\lfloor \ell/B\rfloor, \lfloor r/B\rfloor, t\bigr)$ with $B = n^{2/3}$. Moving `t` forward or back applies or reverts exactly one update — and for that you must have **saved the cell's old value** the instant before overwriting it. The two problems below share that three-pointer skeleton and differ only in payload: CF 940F maintains a *frequency-of-frequency* table to answer a MEX, and a self-authored range-distinct task (whose second slot has no authentic pure-Mo-with-updates judge problem in our offline cache, so it is authored and stressed rather than linked — never fabricated) maintains a plain distinct counter. (A roster note: CF 940F is the flagship Mo-with-updates problem; tree-path variants such as CF 375D use the same value table on a different shape and are cited, not solved, here.)

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **A query is a triple $(\ell, r, t)$.** $t$ counts the updates applied *before* it in input order; carry the original id so answers print in order (@sec-mo-a3).
- **Sort by $\bigl(\lfloor \ell/B\rfloor, \lfloor r/B\rfloor, t\bigr)$ with $B = n^{2/3}$** — not the two-pointer $n/\sqrt q$ — so three pointers balance at $O(n^{5/3})$ (@sec-mo-pit).
- **`apply_time` stashes the old value before overwriting; `revert_time` uses the stash.** Overwrite-without-stash makes the move irreversible.
- **Touch the window only if the changed cell lies inside it.** An update outside $[\ell, r]$ changes the stored value but not the aggregate; both cases must keep the array consistent.
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-940f-machine-learning/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a MEX-of-frequencies to a plain distinct count.** The previous problem kept a `freq`-plus-`ftf` pair and scanned `ftf` for the smallest missing count. The next reuses @sec-mo-a3's already-built three-pointer engine verbatim, but the payload is the simplest one there is — "how many distinct values in $[\ell, r]$" — to show that Mo-with-updates is a *movement discipline*, and the hard part (the time stash) is identical no matter what the window reports.]{.flow-bridge}

### Problem: Distinct values per range with point updates {#sec-mo-p3-distinct}

::: {.p-statement}
*Self-authored (no judge link).* An array $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^{5}$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^{9}$) and $q$ operations of two kinds: a **query** $1\ \ell\ r$ asks for the number of **distinct** values in $a_\ell, \ldots, a_r$, and an **update** $2\ p\ x$ sets $a_p \leftarrow x$. Queries reflect the updates that precede them ($1 \le q \le 10^{5}$).

Example — $a = [1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]$: query $[1,6] = [1,2,3,1,1,2]$ has $\{1,2,3\}$, answer `3`; after update $2\ 2\ 1$ (a $2 \to 1$ at position $2$) the same range $[1,6] = [1,1,3,1,1,2]$ still has $\{1,3,2\}$, answer `3`; after update $2\ 4\ 4$ (a $1 \to 4$ at position $4$) the full range $[1,8] = [1,1,3,4,1,2,2,2]$ has $\{1,3,4,2\}$, answer `4`. Output `3`, `3`, `4`. (Checked against a replay-and-set oracle — the same one @sec-mo-a3 builds — then stressed.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
This is @sec-mo-a3's engine with nothing new to prove: the window already maintains `distinct` via the $0 \to 1$ / $1 \to 0$ edges of `add`/`remove`, so the only addition over classic Mo is the *time* pointer. Applying update $(p, x)$ when $p$ is inside $[\ell, r]$ must first let the old value out of the count and then let the new one in; when $p$ is outside, only the stored cell changes. Because the whole engine — compression, the six movement loops, the stash — is already written and stressed in @sec-mo-a3, we reuse that `mo_with_updates` function directly rather than re-derive it: the pedagogical point is that a single three-pointer skeleton answers any $O(1)$-slidable payload.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Replay and set-size.** Per query, copy the array, apply the first $t$ updates, return $\lvert \operatorname{set}(a[\ell..r]) \rvert$. $O(n)$ per query — the oracle `distinct_replay` from @sec-mo-a3.
2. **Mo with updates.** Call `mo_with_updates(a0, queries, updates)` (defined in @sec-mo-a3): compress values, sort $(\ell, r, t)$ by blocks with $B = n^{2/3}$, keep `freq`/`distinct`, and move $\ell, r, t$ with the stash discipline. $O(n^{5/3})$.

**Invariant.** In `mo_with_updates`, `freq`/`distinct` always describe $[cl, cr]$ after $ct$ updates; each of the six loops moves one pointer by one step and updates the tables in $O(1)$, and `apply_time`/`revert_time` swap a cell's contribution only when that cell is inside the window. When all loops land on $(\ell, r, t)$, `distinct` is the true count over $[\ell, r]$ in that version of the array.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Replay the updates, then take a set size

::: {.form-next}
Per query, copy the array, apply the first $t$ updates, and return the size of $\operatorname{set}(a[\ell..r])$. $O(n)$ per query — reference only; this is `distinct_replay` from @sec-mo-a3.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
# distinct_replay is defined in @sec-mo-a3; here it is the per-query oracle for this task
assert distinct_replay([1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], [(1, 1), (3, 4)], 0, 5, 0) == 3
assert distinct_replay([1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], [(1, 1), (3, 4)], 0, 5, 1) == 3
assert distinct_replay([1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], [(1, 1), (3, 4)], 0, 7, 2) == 4
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: apply the first t updates, then count distinct values in [l, r] with a set
int distinct_ops_brute(const vector<long long>& a0,
                       const vector<pair<int, long long> >& updates, int l, int r, int t) {
    vector<long long> arr = a0;
    for (int k = 0; k < t; ++k) arr[updates[k].first] = updates[k].second;
    set<long long> s;
    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) s.insert(arr[i]);
    return (int)s.size();
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Operations are 1-indexed on the (authored) input and 0-indexed in the code; a query's $t$ is the count of updates that appear before it. Only updates strictly *before* the query are replayed, so ordering matters in the oracle exactly as it does for the engine.

#### Reuse the three-pointer engine (Mo with updates)

::: {.form-next}
Feed `mo_with_updates` (from @sec-mo-a3) the triples $(\ell, r, t)$: it compresses values, sorts by $(\lfloor \ell/B\rfloor, \lfloor r/B\rfloor, t)$ with $B = n^{2/3}$, and maintains `freq`/`distinct` with the stash. $O(n^{5/3})$, no new code.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: sec-mo-p3-distinct-sol
# mo_with_updates (@sec-mo-a3) IS the engine; this task only reads operations into (l, r, t) triples.
a0 = [1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]
ups = [(1, 1), (3, 4)]                 # 0-indexed positions
qs = [(0, 5, 0), (0, 5, 1), (0, 7, 2)]  # t = number of the first updates already applied
assert mo_with_updates(a0, qs, ups) == [3, 3, 4]
for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 40)
    a = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(n)]
    u = random.randint(0, 15)
    updates = [(random.randrange(n), random.randint(0, 5)) for _ in range(u)]
    qq = random.randint(1, 15)
    queries = [(*sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n))), random.randint(0, u))
               for _ in range(qq)]
    assert mo_with_updates(a, queries, updates) == [distinct_replay(a, updates, l, r, t)
                                                     for l, r, t in queries]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// Mo with updates for distinct-count (full program); reuses the same three-pointer skeleton as CF 940F
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    int n, q;
    if (!(cin >> n >> q)) return 0;
    vector<long long> raw(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> raw[i];

    struct Op { int type, l, r; long long x; };
    vector<Op> ops(q);
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) {
        int t; cin >> t;
        if (t == 1) { int l, r; cin >> l >> r; ops[i] = {1, l - 1, r - 1, 0}; }
        else { int p; long long x; cin >> p >> x; ops[i] = {2, p - 1, 0, x}; }
    }
    vector<long long> vals = raw;
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) if (ops[i].type == 2) vals.push_back(ops[i].x);
    sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
    vals.erase(unique(vals.begin(), vals.end()), vals.end());
    vector<int> a(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        a[i] = (int)(lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), raw[i]) - vals.begin());

    vector<array<int, 4> > Q;                    // {l, r, t, id}
    vector<array<long long, 3> > U;              // {pos, newid, old}
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) {
        if (ops[i].type == 1) Q.push_back({ops[i].l, ops[i].r, (int)U.size(), (int)Q.size()});
        else {
            int nid = (int)(lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), ops[i].x) - vals.begin());
            U.push_back({ops[i].l, nid, 0});
        }
    }
    int M = (int)Q.size();
    if (M == 0) return 0;
    int B = max(1, (int)pow((double)n, 2.0 / 3.0));
    sort(Q.begin(), Q.end(), [B](const array<int,4>& x, const array<int,4>& y) {
        if (x[0] / B != y[0] / B) return x[0] / B < y[0] / B;
        if (x[1] / B != y[1] / B) return x[1] / B < y[1] / B;
        return x[2] < y[2];
    });
    vector<int> freq(vals.size(), 0);
    vector<long long> ans(M);
    int distinct = 0, cl = 0, cr = -1, ct = 0;
    auto add_val = [&](int v) { if (++freq[v] == 1) distinct++; };
    auto rem_val = [&](int v) { if (--freq[v] == 0) distinct--; };
    auto apply_time = [&]() {
        int pos = (int)U[ct][0]; int nid = (int)U[ct][1];
        U[ct][2] = a[pos];
        if (cl <= pos && pos <= cr) { rem_val(a[pos]); add_val(nid); }
        a[pos] = nid;
        ct++;
    };
    auto revert_time = [&]() {
        ct--;
        int pos = (int)U[ct][0]; int oldid = (int)U[ct][2];
        if (cl <= pos && pos <= cr) { rem_val(a[pos]); add_val(oldid); }
        a[pos] = oldid;
    };
    for (int qi = 0; qi < M; ++qi) {
        int l = Q[qi][0], r = Q[qi][1], t = Q[qi][2], id = Q[qi][3];
        while (cr < r) add_val(a[++cr]);
        while (cl > l) add_val(a[--cl]);
        while (cl < l) rem_val(a[cl++]);
        while (cr > r) rem_val(a[cr--]);
        while (ct < t) apply_time();
        while (ct > t) revert_time();
        ans[id] = distinct;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < M; ++i) cout << ans[i] << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `add_val`/`rem_val` now carry the *distinct* payload (`freq` crossing $0$ moves the counter) instead of the `ftf` table, yet every surrounding line — compression, the $(\ell,r,t)$ sort, the guarded `apply_time`/`revert_time`, the stash in `U[ct][2]` — is byte-for-byte the CF 940F skeleton. That identity is the lesson: swapping the two $O(1)$ lambdas is the only change a new answer needs. Printing `ans[id]` in input order is the offline discipline again (@sec-mo-pit).
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Replay:** $O(n)$ per query, $O(nq)$ reference only. **Mo with updates:** $O(n^{5/3})$ with $B = n^{2/3}$, space $O(n + |\text{distinct values}|)$ — identical envelope to CF 940F; only the per-move payload differs.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Update with the *same* value ($x = a_p$): applying it is a no-op on the tables but still consumes a stash slot; correctness is unaffected.
- Position updated outside the window: `freq`/`distinct` untouched; the stored cell must still change so a later slide reads the new value.
- All-equal range after updates: `distinct` collapses to $1$; the $0\to1$ guard on the counter is the whole payload.
- Reverting must pop the stash in exact reverse of applying — the shared `ct` pointer guarantees the pairing (@sec-mo-a3).
:::
