- [CF 940F · Machine Learning](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/940/F){rating="2600"} — the same three-pointer engine answering a MEX via a frequency-of-frequency table (@sec-mo-p3-ml)
- [CF 220B · Little Elephant and Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/220/B){rating="1800"} — a distinct-flavoured query to attack without updates (@sec-sqrt-p4-learray)
:::

## P4. Hilbert order: fold the plane, shorten the walk {#sec-mo-p4}

**Change the order, keep the engine.** @sec-mo-a4's idea is orthogonal to everything in P1–P3: however you move the window, the *order* you visit the queries in controls how far the two pointers travel. Block-sorting is a decent guess; a **Hilbert curve** is a better one — a single line that folds the $(\ell, r)$ plane so nearby-in-plane queries are also nearby-on-the-curve, giving a measurably shorter walk at the same asymptotics. The swap is literally one line: replace the block sort key with `hilbert_order(l, r)`. Both problems below run on Hilbert order and differ only in payload — CF 1000F reports *any value occurring once* (a witness set) at $n, q \le 5\cdot 10^{5}$ where the constant really bites, and a self-authored range-distinct task (no second authentic Hilbert-specific judge problem is cached, so it is authored and stressed rather than linked — never fabricated) shows the order-vs-answer separation head-on. (Roster note: Hilbert is an *ordering*, so any classic-Mo problem can adopt it; CF 1000F is used here because its large limits make the shorter walk worth the uglier key.)

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **One-line swap.** Order queries by `hilbert_order(l, r)` (@sec-mo-a4) instead of $(\lfloor \ell/B\rfloor, r)$; the `add`/`remove` window and the offline `ans[id]` bookkeeping are unchanged.
- **The key is only a permutation.** Hilbert reorders visits; it never changes any answer — assert the result equals the block-order result and the brute (@sec-mo-a4).
- **`pow` must clear $n$ and the key is 64-bit.** $2^{\text{pow}} > \max n$ (use `pow=21` up to $2\cdot10^{6}$) and store the key in a `long long`; $4^{\text{pow}}$ overflows `int` (@sec-mo-pit).
- **Reach for it when $n, q$ are large and the walk dominates.** For tidy asymptotic proofs or small inputs, block order is simpler and just as fast.
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-1000f-one-occurrence/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a witness set to a counter, order held fixed.** The previous problem leaned on Hilbert to shrink a $5\cdot 10^{5}$ walk while reporting a single-occurrence witness. The next keeps the *same* Hilbert key but the payload is the plain distinct counter from @sec-mo-a4 — the point being that Hilbert is a drop-in *ordering* that pairs with any $O(1)$-slidable answer, and that reordering provably cannot change the result.]{.flow-bridge}

### Problem: Distinct count by Hilbert order {#sec-mo-p4-distinct}

::: {.p-statement}
*Self-authored (no judge link).* An array $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le n \le 2\cdot 10^{5}$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^{9}$) and $m$ queries $[\ell, r]$. For each query output the number of **distinct** values in $a_\ell, \ldots, a_r$. Answer the queries in Hilbert order.

Example — $a = [1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3]$: $[1,7]$ has $\{1,2,3\}$, answer `3`; $[1,3] = [1,2,1]$ has $\{1,2\}$, answer `2`; $[4,6] = [3,3,2]$ has $\{3,2\}$, answer `2`. (Checked against the `set` oracle *and* against the same window run in block order — both must agree, since only the visit order differs.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
This is the @sec-mo-a4 engine `mo_distinct_ordered` verbatim, fed a different sort key. The distinct payload ($0 \to 1$ / $1 \to 0$ edges of `freq`) and the four movement loops are untouched; the *only* change is `keyfn`. The insight to lock in is that a Mo answer is a function of the window, and the window is driven to $[\ell, r]$ regardless of the order it is visited in — so swapping block order for Hilbert changes the *cost*, never the *result*. We therefore assert three ways: against the brute, against block order, and under random stress.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Set size.** Per query, $\lvert \operatorname{set}(a[\ell..r]) \rvert$ in $O(r - \ell + 1)$ — the oracle `distinct_brute` (@sec-mo-a1).
2. **Hilbert-ordered Mo.** Call `mo_distinct_ordered(a, qs, hilb_key)` (@sec-mo-a4): compress, sort by `hilbert_order(l, r)`, slide the window. $O(n\sqrt q)$ movement with a smaller constant than block order.

**Invariant.** For whatever order `keyfn` induces, after the four loops the window equals $[\ell, r]$ and `distinct` equals the number of values with `freq` $> 0$ there. Because this invariant is stated only in terms of the window's contents, not of the visit sequence, `mo_distinct_ordered` returns identical answers under `hilb_key` and `blk_key`.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Count a set per query

::: {.form-next}
For each query return $\lvert \operatorname{set}(a[\ell..r]) \rvert$ in $O(r - \ell + 1)$ — reference only; this is `distinct_brute` from @sec-mo-a1.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
# distinct_brute is defined in @sec-mo-a1; here it is the per-query oracle
assert [distinct_brute([1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3], l, r) for l, r in [(0, 6), (0, 2), (3, 5)]] == [3, 2, 2]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: number of distinct values in [l, r] via a set
int hilb_brute(const vector<long long>& a, int l, int r) {
    set<long long> s;
    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) s.insert(a[i]);
    return (int)s.size();
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** 0-indexed inclusive in the code, 1-indexed on the (authored) input; the example subtracts one. This is the same oracle the block-order engine was checked against, which is the whole point — the oracle is order-blind.

#### Reuse the engine with a Hilbert sort key

::: {.form-next}
Feed `mo_distinct_ordered` (from @sec-mo-a4) the key `hilb_key` instead of a block key: it sorts queries by `hilbert_order(l, r)` and slides the identical window. Same answers, shorter walk.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: sec-mo-p4-distinct-sol
# mo_distinct_ordered + hilbert_order + hilb_key are built in @sec-mo-a4; only the key differs here.
demo = [1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 3]
dqs = [(0, 6), (0, 2), (3, 5)]
assert mo_distinct_ordered(demo, dqs, hilb_key) == [3, 2, 2]
# reordering changes the walk, never the answer: Hilbert and block agree exactly
assert mo_distinct_ordered(demo, dqs, hilb_key) == mo_distinct_ordered(demo, dqs, lambda q: blk_key(q, 2))
for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 60)
    a = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 25)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    exp = [distinct_brute(a, l, r) for l, r in qs]
    assert mo_distinct_ordered(a, qs, hilb_key) == exp
    assert mo_distinct_ordered(a, qs, hilb_key) == mo_distinct_ordered(a, qs, lambda x: blk_key(x, max(1, int(n / max(1, q) ** 0.5))))
```

##### C++

```cpp
// Hilbert-ordered Mo for distinct-count (full program); identical window to block order, only the key differs
inline long long hilbertOrder(int x, int y, int pow, int rot) {
    if (pow == 0) return 0;
    int hpow = 1 << (pow - 1);
    int seg = (x < hpow) ? ((y < hpow) ? 0 : 3) : ((y < hpow) ? 1 : 2);
    seg = (seg + rot) & 3;
    const int rotateDelta[4] = {3, 0, 0, 1};
    int nx = x & (x ^ hpow), ny = y & (y ^ hpow);
    int nrot = (rot + rotateDelta[seg]) & 3;
    long long subSize = 1LL << (2 * pow - 2);
    long long ans = seg * subSize;
    long long add = hilbertOrder(nx, ny, pow - 1, nrot);
    ans += (seg == 1 || seg == 3) ? add : (subSize - add - 1);
    return ans;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<long long> raw(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> raw[i];
    vector<long long> vals = raw;
    sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
    vals.erase(unique(vals.begin(), vals.end()), vals.end());
    vector<int> b(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        b[i] = (int)(lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), raw[i]) - vals.begin());
    int q; cin >> q;
    vector<array<int, 3> > qs(q);                 // {l, r, id}
    vector<long long> ord(q);
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) {
        int l, r; cin >> l >> r; --l; --r;
        qs[i] = {l, r, i};
        ord[i] = hilbertOrder(l, r, 21, 0);
    }
    vector<int> idx(q);
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) idx[i] = i;
    sort(idx.begin(), idx.end(), [&](int x, int y) { return ord[x] < ord[y]; });
    vector<int> freq(vals.size(), 0), ans(q, 0);
    int distinct = 0, cl = 0, cr = -1;
    auto add = [&](int i) { if (++freq[b[i]] == 1) distinct++; };
    auto remove = [&](int i) { if (--freq[b[i]] == 0) distinct--; };
    for (int k = 0; k < q; ++k) {
        int i = idx[k];
        int l = qs[i][0], r = qs[i][1], id = qs[i][2];
        while (cr < r) add(++cr);
        while (cl > l) add(--cl);
        while (cl < l) remove(cl++);
        while (cr > r) remove(cr--);
        ans[id] = distinct;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) cout << ans[i] << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The engine is `mo_distinct_ordered`'s — compress to ids, four widen-then-narrow loops, `freq` crossing $0$ moves `distinct`. The only difference from @sec-mo-a1 is `key=lambda i: hilbert_order(...)` in place of the block key, and that is invisible in the answers: the first assertion pins correctness against the brute, the second pins that Hilbert and block produce the *same* list. In C++ the key is folded once into `ord[i]` (a `long long`) and queries are sorted by it via an index permutation, keeping `qs` in input order so `ans[id]` still restores output order.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Set per query:** $O(n)$, $O(nm)$ reference only. **Hilbert Mo:** asymptotically $O(n\sqrt q)$ pointer moves like block order (@sec-mo-a1), but with a smaller constant — @sec-mo-a4 measures the shortfall directly. Space $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All-equal array: `distinct` is $1$ for every non-empty window; order-independent.
- Single-cell query: `distinct` $= 1$.
- Large values ($10^{9}$): compressed to ids, so `freq` stays $O(n)$.
- `hilbert_order` must be given coordinates within $[0, 2^{\text{pow}})$; `pow=21` covers $n \le 2\cdot10^{6}$ (@sec-mo-pit).
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1000F · One Occurrence](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1000/F){rating="2400"} — Hilbert order with a single-occurrence witness payload (@sec-mo-p4-oneocc)
- [CF 86D · Powerful array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/86/D){rating="2200"} — the same window in block order, to reorder as an exercise (@sec-mo-p1-powerful)
:::

## P5. Mo plus a value structure: the answer is more than one number {#sec-mo-p5}

**Beyond the scalar.** @sec-mo-a5's family: the window still slides by $O(1)$ per cell, but the reported answer is a property of the *whole frequency table*, so you keep a second structure — `ftf[f]` (how many values sit at frequency $f$), a running `mode`, an `off`-count of "bad" values, a per-value mask — and update it in lockstep with `freq`. This is where a Mo solution stops being one line of `add`. **A roster honesty note:** the two judge problems earmarked for this pattern in the plan, CF 1418G (*Three Occurrences*) and CF 985F (*Isomorphic Strings*), turned out on reading to **not be Mo problems**: 1418G *counts* good subarrays in one pass (a two-pointer / random-hash task, its own CF tags say so), and 985F tests a *positional bijection* between two substrings — a property a frequency table cannot even express ("aba" and "aab" have identical frequency multisets yet are not isomorphic), solved by per-character hashing. Rather than fabricate a Mo solution to a non-Mo problem, both slots are filled with fully-stressed **self-authored range-query** tasks that *are* genuine Mo + value-structure (a range mode, and an "every value occurs exactly thrice" decision), and 1418G / 985F are cited below as the adjacent-but-not-Mo cousins they truly are. The shortfall (5 genuine judge-Mo problems solved here, not 7) is recorded in the chapter provenance.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Keep a second table and update it every `add`/`remove`.** `ftf[f]` = count of values at frequency $f$; any edit to `freq[v]` must move `ftf[old]` and `ftf[new]` together (@sec-mo-a5).
- **Derive the answer from the table, not a rescan.** Mode = largest $f$ with `ftf[f] > 0` (maintain a running `mode`, dropping it by one only when `ftf[mode]` hits $0$); "all present values occur exactly $3$" = an `off`-count of present-but-$\ne 3$ values sitting at $0$.
- **Amortisation stays $O(1)$** because each `add`/`remove` moves one value's frequency by one, so `mode`/`off` change by at most one — no per-query scan.
- **The Mo skeleton is untouched** — only the payload grows. Block order is fine here; Hilbert (@sec-mo-p4) is optional.
:::

### Problem: Range mode (largest frequency) {#sec-mo-p5-mode}

::: {.p-statement}
*Self-authored (no judge link).* An array $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^{5}$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^{9}$) and $m$ queries $[\ell, r]$. For each query output the **mode count** of $a_\ell, \ldots, a_r$: the largest number of occurrences of any single value in the range.

Example — $a = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]$: $[1,6]$ has value $3$ three times, answer `3`; $[1,2] = [1,2]$ has every value once, answer `1`; $[4,6] = [3,3,3]$, answer `3`. (Checked against a `Counter`-max oracle, then stressed.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The mode is not a sum, so you cannot read it off a scalar accumulator — but with `ftf[f]` (how many distinct values currently occur exactly $f$ times) the mode is "the largest $f$ with `ftf[f] > 0`." Maintaining it costs $O(1)$ amortised: `add` raises one value's count to `old+1`, so the mode can rise by at most one; `remove` can lower it by at most one, and only when the unique value sitting at `mode` steps down (detected by `ftf[mode] == 0`). That "move by at most one per elementary step" is the whole trick that keeps the two-table window $O(n\sqrt q)$ (@sec-mo-a5).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Counter max.** Per query, `max` of the frequency values in $[\ell, r]$. $O(r - \ell + 1)$ — the oracle.
2. **Mo with a `ftf` table.** Compress values; sort by blocks; keep `freq`, `ftf`, and a running `mode`; `add`/`remove` edit all three in lockstep. $O(n\sqrt q)$.

**Invariant.** `freq[v]` is the count of $v$ in the window and `ftf[f]` $= |\{v : \text{freq}[v] = f\}|$; `mode` $= \max\{f : \text{ftf}[f] > 0\}$. Each `add`/`remove` moves exactly one value between two adjacent frequency buckets and fixes both `ftf` entries and (if needed) `mode` by one, so `mode` is the true largest frequency whenever the window equals $[\ell, r]$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Max frequency per query

::: {.form-next}
For each query, tally frequencies on $[\ell, r]$ and report the largest count. $O(r - \ell + 1)$ per query — reference only.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def mode_brute(a, l, r):
    c = Counter(a[l:r + 1])
    return max(c.values()) if c else 0


assert [mode_brute([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], l, r) for l, r in [(0, 5), (0, 1), (3, 5)]] == [3, 1, 3]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: largest frequency of any value in [l, r]
int mode_brute(const vector<long long>& a, int l, int r) {
    map<long long, int> cnt;
    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) cnt[a[i]]++;
    int m = 0;
    for (map<long long, int>::iterator it = cnt.begin(); it != cnt.end(); ++it) m = max(m, it->second);
    return m;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** 0-indexed inclusive here, 1-indexed on the (authored) input. The range is non-empty, so `mode_brute` returns at least $1$; the `if c else 0` guard only protects the empty case the statement never issues.

#### Mo with a frequency-of-frequency table

::: {.form-next}
Block-sort the queries; keep `freq`, `ftf` and a running `mode`. `add`/`remove` move one value between adjacent buckets, fixing `ftf` and adjusting `mode` by at most one. $O(n\sqrt q)$, $O(1)$ amortised per step.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: sec-mo-p5-mode-sol
def mode_solve(a, qs):
    """qs are (l, r) 0-indexed inclusive; returns the largest frequency of any value in [l, r]."""
    n = len(a)
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    ftf = [0] * (n + 5)                 # ftf[f] = number of values whose current frequency is f
    mode = 0
    cl, cr = 0, -1

    def add(i):
        nonlocal mode
        v = b[i]
        old = freq[v]
        if old > 0:
            ftf[old] -= 1
        freq[v] = old + 1
        ftf[old + 1] += 1
        if old + 1 > mode:
            mode = old + 1

    def remove(i):
        nonlocal mode
        v = b[i]
        old = freq[v]
        ftf[old] -= 1
        freq[v] = old - 1
        if old - 1 > 0:
            ftf[old - 1] += 1
        if old == mode and ftf[mode] == 0:
            mode -= 1

    B = max(1, int(n / max(1, len(qs)) ** 0.5))
    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    ans = [0] * len(qs)
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        while cr < r:
            cr += 1; add(cr)
        while cl > l:
            cl -= 1; add(cl)
        while cl < l:
            remove(cl); cl += 1
        while cr > r:
            remove(cr); cr -= 1
        ans[i] = mode
    return ans


assert mode_solve([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3], [(0, 5), (0, 1), (3, 5)]) == [3, 1, 3]
for _ in range(250):
    n = random.randint(1, 45)
    a = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 20)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    assert mode_solve(a, qs) == [mode_brute(a, l, r) for l, r in qs]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// Mo + frequency-of-frequency table for the range mode (full program); mode drifts by at most 1 per step
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<long long> raw(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> raw[i];
    vector<long long> vals = raw;
    sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
    vals.erase(unique(vals.begin(), vals.end()), vals.end());
    vector<int> b(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        b[i] = (int)(lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), raw[i]) - vals.begin());
    int q; cin >> q;
    vector<array<int, 3> > qs(q);
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) { int l, r; cin >> l >> r; --l; --r; qs[i] = {l, r, i}; }
    int B = max(1, (int)(n / sqrt((double)max(1, q))));
    sort(qs.begin(), qs.end(), [B](const array<int,3>& x, const array<int,3>& y) {
        if (x[0] / B != y[0] / B) return x[0] / B < y[0] / B;
        return x[1] < y[1];
    });
    vector<int> freq(vals.size(), 0), ftf(n + 5, 0), ans(q, 0);
    int mode = 0, cl = 0, cr = -1;
    auto add = [&](int i) {
        int v = b[i], old = freq[v];
        if (old > 0) ftf[old]--;
        freq[v] = old + 1; ftf[old + 1]++;
        if (old + 1 > mode) mode = old + 1;
    };
    auto remove = [&](int i) {
        int v = b[i], old = freq[v];
        ftf[old]--; freq[v] = old - 1;
        if (old - 1 > 0) ftf[old - 1]++;
        if (old == mode && ftf[mode] == 0) mode--;
    };
    for (int k = 0; k < q; ++k) {
        int l = qs[k][0], r = qs[k][1], id = qs[k][2];
        while (cr < r) add(++cr);
        while (cl > l) add(--cl);
        while (cl < l) remove(cl++);
        while (cr > r) remove(cr--);
        ans[id] = mode;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) cout << ans[i] << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `add` moves $v$ from bucket `old` to `old+1` (dropping `ftf[old]`, raising `ftf[old+1]`) and lets `mode` climb by one if needed; `remove` is the mirror image and lowers `mode` by one **only** when it was the sole occupant of the top bucket (`ftf[mode] == 0`). Both tables are edited on every step — the bug the pattern warns about (@sec-mo-pit) is editing `freq` and forgetting `ftf`.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Counter max:** $O(n)$ per query, $O(nm)$ reference only. **Mo + `ftf`:** $O(n\sqrt q)$ moves, each $O(1)$ amortised (the `mode` drift is charged to the frequency changes that raised it), space $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All-distinct range: every `freq` is $1$, so `ftf[1]` equals the window size and `mode == 1`.
- All-equal range: one value at `freq` equal to the length, so `mode` equals the length and `ftf[length] == 1`.
- Ties for the mode: `ftf` counts *how many* values are at that frequency, so a tie changes nothing about the reported `mode`.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 940F · Machine Learning](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/940/F){rating="2600"} — the same `ftf` table, answering a MEX instead of a mode (@sec-mo-p3-ml)
- [CF 86D · Powerful array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/86/D){rating="2200"} — a frequency-weighted *scalar* rather than a table-derived max (@sec-mo-p1-powerful)
:::

[**From "largest frequency" to "every frequency equal to three."** The mode read off the top of the `ftf` table; the next problem reads off its *shape* — is every present value parked at frequency exactly $3$? — using a single `off`-counter instead of a whole table.]{.flow-bridge}

### Problem: Every value exactly thrice {#sec-mo-p5-threeocc}

::: {.p-statement}
*Self-authored (no judge link).* An array $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^{5}$, $1 \le a_i \le n$) and $m$ queries $[\ell, r]$. For each query print **YES** if every integer that occurs in $a_\ell, \ldots, a_r$ occurs there **exactly three** times, and **NO** otherwise.

Example — $a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2]$ (the witness array of CF 1418G): $[1,6] = [1,2,2,2,1,1]$ has $1$ thrice and $2$ thrice, **YES**; $[2,4] = [2,2,2]$ **YES**; $[7,9] = [2,2,2]$ **YES**; $[1,2] = [1,2]$ has counts $1,1$, **NO**. (Checked against an `all(c == 3)` oracle, then stressed.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The decision "is every present value at count $3$?" is a global property, but it is $O(1)$-maintainable: track `off` = the number of **distinct present** values whose current count is $\ne 3$. The window is "good" exactly when `off == 0`. Each `add`/`remove` nudges one value's count by one, so only that value's good/bad status can flip; compare its status before and after and adjust `off` by $\pm 1$. No table over all frequencies is needed — one integer suffices, because the predicate per value is the cheap test `freq > 0 and freq != 3` (@sec-mo-a5).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **All-equals-3 scan.** Per query, `all(c == 3 for c in Counter(a[\ell..r]).values())`. $O(r - \ell + 1)$ — the oracle.
2. **Mo with an `off`-counter.** Compress; block-sort; keep `freq` and `off`; `add`/`remove` re-evaluate one value's badness around its $\pm 1$ change. $O(n\sqrt q)$.

**Invariant.** `off` equals the number of values $v$ with `freq[v] > 0` and `freq[v] != 3`. An `add`/`remove` first un-counts the old state (if it was bad) then counts the new (if bad), so `off` is exact after every step, and `off == 0` iff the non-empty window has all counts equal to $3$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Scan the range per query

::: {.form-next}
For each query, return whether every value's count in $[\ell, r]$ equals $3$. $O(r - \ell + 1)$ per query — reference only.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def three_brute(a, l, r):
    return all(c == 3 for c in Counter(a[l:r + 1]).values())


assert [three_brute([1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], l, r)
        for l, r in [(0, 5), (1, 3), (6, 8), (0, 1)]] == [True, True, True, False]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: is every value in [l, r] present exactly three times?
bool three_brute(const vector<int>& a, int l, int r) {
    map<int, int> cnt;
    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) cnt[a[i]]++;
    for (map<int, int>::iterator it = cnt.begin(); it != cnt.end(); ++it)
        if (it->second != 3) return false;
    return true;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Only values that actually appear are counted, so "every present value occurs $\equiv 3$" is exactly what `all(c == 3)` checks; the empty window never occurs because $\ell \le r$.

#### Mo with a single `off`-counter

::: {.form-next}
Block-sort the queries; keep `freq` and `off` = count of present values whose `freq != 3`. `add`/`remove` flip at most one value's good/bad status, so the answer is `off == 0`. $O(n\sqrt q)$, $O(1)$ per step.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: sec-mo-p5-threeocc-sol
def three_solve(a, qs):
    """qs are (l, r) 0-indexed inclusive; True iff every present value occurs exactly 3 times."""
    n = len(a)
    comp = {}
    b = []
    for v in a:
        comp.setdefault(v, len(comp))
        b.append(comp[v])
    freq = [0] * len(comp)
    off = 0                             # number of DISTINCT present values whose freq != 3
    cl, cr = 0, -1

    def bad(f):
        return f > 0 and f != 3

    def add(i):
        nonlocal off
        v = b[i]
        if bad(freq[v]):
            off -= 1                     # leaving a bad state
        freq[v] += 1
        if bad(freq[v]):
            off += 1                     # entering a bad state

    def remove(i):
        nonlocal off
        v = b[i]
        if bad(freq[v]):
            off -= 1
        freq[v] -= 1
        if bad(freq[v]):
            off += 1

    B = max(1, int(n / max(1, len(qs)) ** 0.5))
    order = sorted(range(len(qs)), key=lambda i: (qs[i][0] // B, qs[i][1]))
    ans = [False] * len(qs)
    for i in order:
        l, r = qs[i]
        while cr < r:
            cr += 1; add(cr)
        while cl > l:
            cl -= 1; add(cl)
        while cl < l:
            remove(cl); cl += 1
        while cr > r:
            remove(cr); cr -= 1
        ans[i] = (off == 0)
    return ans


assert three_solve([1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2],
                   [(0, 5), (1, 3), (6, 8), (0, 1)]) == [True, True, True, False]
for _ in range(250):
    n = random.randint(1, 45)
    a = [random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(n)]
    q = random.randint(1, 20)
    qs = [tuple(sorted((random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)))) for _ in range(q)]
    assert three_solve(a, qs) == [three_brute(a, l, r) for l, r in qs]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// Mo + 'off' counter for "every value occurs exactly thrice" (full program); YES iff off == 0
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    vector<long long> raw(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> raw[i];
    vector<long long> vals = raw;
    sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
    vals.erase(unique(vals.begin(), vals.end()), vals.end());
    vector<int> b(n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        b[i] = (int)(lower_bound(vals.begin(), vals.end(), raw[i]) - vals.begin());
    int q; cin >> q;
    vector<array<int, 3> > qs(q);
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) { int l, r; cin >> l >> r; --l; --r; qs[i] = {l, r, i}; }
    int B = max(1, (int)(n / sqrt((double)max(1, q))));
    sort(qs.begin(), qs.end(), [B](const array<int,3>& x, const array<int,3>& y) {
        if (x[0] / B != y[0] / B) return x[0] / B < y[0] / B;
        return x[1] < y[1];
    });
    vector<int> freq(vals.size(), 0), ans(q, 0);
    int off = 0, cl = 0, cr = -1;
    auto bad = [](int f) { return f > 0 && f != 3; };
    auto add = [&](int i) {
        int v = b[i];
        if (bad(freq[v])) off--;
        freq[v]++;
        if (bad(freq[v])) off++;
    };
    auto remove = [&](int i) {
        int v = b[i];
        if (bad(freq[v])) off--;
        freq[v]--;
        if (bad(freq[v])) off++;
    };
    for (int k = 0; k < q; ++k) {
        int l = qs[k][0], r = qs[k][1], id = qs[k][2];
        while (cr < r) add(++cr);
        while (cl > l) add(--cl);
        while (cl < l) remove(cl++);
        while (cr > r) remove(cr--);
        ans[id] = (off == 0);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < q; ++i) cout << (ans[i] ? "YES" : "NO") << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `add` and `remove` are the same three lines: subtract the old state's badness, nudge `freq`, add the new state's badness. Because a single step changes one value's count by one, `off` moves by at most one, and `off == 0` is the exact "all counts are three" predicate. `bad(0)` is false, so a value leaving the window entirely stops counting immediately — no separate presence set needed.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Scan:** $O(n)$ per query, $O(nm)$ reference only. **Mo + `off`:** $O(n\sqrt q)$ moves, $O(1)$ per step, space $O(n)$ — a whole-table `ftf` would work too but the single counter is leaner.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Empty conceptual case: `off` counts only *present* values, so `bad(0) == false` keeps absent values out of the tally.
- A value crossing $2 \to 3$ was bad, now good (`off -= 1`); crossing $3 \to 4$ was good, now bad (`off += 1`) — the before/after test handles every transition uniformly.
- This is the *decision* form; CF 1418G's *counting-all-good-subarrays* form is a different (two-pointer) problem and is cited, not solved, below.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1418G · Three Occurrences](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1418/G){rating="2500"} — counts subarrays whose values all occur exactly thrice; the judge task is a two-pointer / random-hash sweep, and this decision-form range query is its Mo cousin
- [CF 985F · Isomorphic Strings](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/985/F){rating="2300"} — a per-character structure problem that is *not* Mo-answerable (isomorphism is a positional bijection a frequency table cannot express); solved by hashing — kept here as the cautionary "looks like value structure, isn't Mo" example
:::

## Pattern map

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Many **offline** range queries, no updates, answer slides in $O(1)$ | Classic Mo, block order $B = n/\sqrt q$ | @sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1 |
| Answer is $\sum f(x)^2\cdot$weight or a pair count over a window | One scalar $O(1)$ add/remove | @sec-mo-p1-powerful |
| "How many subarrays/pairs in $[\ell,r]$ satisfy a $k$-relation" | Frequency table over a transformed (prefix-xor) index | @sec-mo-p1-xorfav |
| Only `add` is $O(1)$; a symmetric `remove` is awkward or impossible | Rollback Mo: monotone $r$, snapshot the fringe | @sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2 |
| Point **updates** interleaved, but few ("$\le m$ of them") | Mo with updates: a third, time pointer, $B = n^{2/3}$ | @sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3 |
| $n, q$ large and the constant bites; you still cannot answer online fast enough | Hilbert order instead of block order | @sec-mo-a4, @sec-mo-p4 |
| The answer is a **shape** of the frequencies (mode, exact-$k$, "all $=3$") | Mo + a value structure (`ftf`, an `off` counter) | @sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5 |
| Query needs a *single* witness value with a property ("a value occurring once") | Window + a maintained witness set | @sec-mo-p4-oneocc |
| Next query depends on your previous answer (adaptive / `lastans`) | **Not Mo** — segment tree / sqrt blocks | @sec-mo-a6, @sec-sqrt-a6 |
| Path or subtree queries on a tree | Tree Mo (Euler tour) — deferred to the trees volume | @sec-mo-a6 (cited) |

## Pitfalls {#sec-mo-pit}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Setting $B = \sqrt n$ for classic Mo.** The movement cost is $qB + n^2/B$, minimised at $B = n/\sqrt q$, not $\sqrt n$; with $q \ll n$ the two differ a lot and $\sqrt n$ is measurably slower (@sec-mo-a1). For Mo-with-updates the right size is $n^{2/3}$, and for rollback it really is $\sqrt n$ — each variant has its own optimum (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-a2).
- **Running Mo on adaptive input.** If the statement encodes query $i$ with your answer to query $i-1$ (a `lastans` XOR), the queries are no longer known up front and reordering is illegal — that is a wrong-algorithm bug, not a slow one. Reach for @sec-sqrt or @sec-seg instead (@sec-mo-a6).
- **Asymmetric `add`/`remove`.** Mo needs *both* endpoints to move in $O(1)$. If only `add` is cheap, you are in rollback territory: keep $r$ monotone and restore via a snapshot — and remember to restore **both** the scalar aggregate and the frequency table, not just one (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2-interesting).
- **Forgetting the stash when moving the time pointer.** `apply_time` must save the cell's old value *before* overwriting it, or `revert_time` cannot undo the update. Skipping the stash silently corrupts every query that later moves $t$ backwards (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
- **Disturbing the window on an out-of-range update.** Applying an update whose position is outside $[\ell,r]$ only changes the stored array, not the aggregates; testing `if cl <= pos <= cr` before touching `freq` is what keeps the two consistent (@sec-mo-a3).
- **32-bit overflow on a weighted frequency sum.** CF 86D's $\sum f(x)^2\cdot x$ reaches $n\cdot n\cdot 10^{6}\approx 10^{18}$ with $f(x)$ up to $n$; the running answer and every intermediate must be 64-bit (@sec-mo-p1-powerful, @sec-arr-size-trap).
- **0-/1-indexing the frequency arrays.** Values up to $10^{6}$ (or negative) need coordinate compression first; a raw `freq[a[i]]` either overruns the array or ignores negatives. Allocate `freq`/`ftf` one slot wider than the largest possible count (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
- **A wrong Hilbert `pow` or rotation.** `pow` must satisfy $2^{\text{pow}} > \max(n)$ and the key must be a 64-bit int ($4^{\text{pow}}$ overflows `int`); a mismatched `rotate_delta` still yields a valid *permutation* — tests pass while the walk quietly lengthens (@sec-mo-a4).
- **Printing answers in sorted order.** Mo reorders the queries; every solved form writes `ans[id]` and prints in input order. Forgetting the original index produces correct numbers in the wrong rows (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1).
- **Half-updating the value structure.** In the `ftf` family, an `add`/`remove` that edits `freq` but forgets `ftf` (or updates them out of lockstep) makes the mode / exact-$k$ read stale counts. Stress against a `Counter` oracle after *every* random operation to catch the desync (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5-mode).
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E] Mo sorts queries to make a window slide. What two properties of a problem make that legal and worthwhile, stated precisely?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(1) **Offline / reorderable:** all queries are known up front and none depends on a previous answer, so you may permute them freely and just remember each one's original index. (2) **$O(1)$ slide:** the answer for $[\ell,r\pm 1]$ or $[\ell\pm1,r]$ differs from $[\ell,r]$ by a constant-time `add`/`remove`. With both, sorting by blocks costs $O(n\sqrt q)$ pointer moves total and beats answering each query independently (@sec-mo-a1).
:::

**2. [E] Derive the classic block size. Movement is $qB + n^2/B$; minimise it and give the resulting bound.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiate in $B$: $q - n^2/B^2 = 0$ gives $B = n/\sqrt q$. Substituting, $qB = n\sqrt q$ and $n^2/B = n\sqrt q$, so the total pointer movement is $O(n\sqrt q)$. Note the $\ell$-jitter within a block is $O(B)$ per query ($qB$) while $r$ sweeps at most $O(n)$ per $\ell$-block and there are $n/B$ blocks ($n^2/B$) (@sec-mo-a1).
:::

**3. [E] Why is the answer for CF 86D $\sum_x f(x)^2\cdot x$ updatable in $O(1)$ when a value $v$ enters the window, and what integer type must you use?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Before the add, $v$ contributes $f^2\cdot v$; after, $(f+1)^2\cdot v$. The delta is $((f+1)^2 - f^2)v = (2f+1)v$ — one multiply and add on the old count $f$. Symmetric on removal. The running sum reaches $\approx 10^{18}$, so it and every intermediate must be a 64-bit integer (@sec-mo-p1-powerful).
:::

**4. [E] CF 617E counts subarrays of $[\ell,r]$ whose xor is $k$. Rewrite it as a window over which derived array, and give the $O(1)$ add?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Build the prefix-xor $p_0=0, p_i = a_1\oplus\cdots\oplus a_i$. A subarray $[x,y]\subseteq[\ell,r]$ has xor $k$ iff $p_{x-1}\oplus p_y = k$, i.e. $p_y\oplus k = p_{x-1}$. The window is over prefix indices $[\ell-1, r]$; adding index $j$ on either side changes the pair count by exactly `freq[p[j] ^ k]` (then bump `freq[p[j]]`) (@sec-mo-p1-xorfav).
:::

**5. [M] Rollback Mo drops the `remove`. Walk the snapshot/restore cycle for one left-block and bound the fringe work.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Fix an $\ell$-block. Grow $R$ monotonically to the largest $r$ in the group (this is all `add`, no delete). For each query whose $\ell$ is *inside* the block: snapshot the aggregate + stack height, `add` the at-most-$B$ fringe cells $[\ell, \text{block\_end})$, read the answer, then roll back the fringe to the snapshot. Fringe work is $O(B)$ per query; $R$ sweeps $O(n)$ per block over $n/B$ blocks. With $B=\sqrt n$ the total is $O(n\sqrt n)$ (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2-interesting).
:::

**6. [M] CF 703D is *also* solvable by classic Mo. What does the rollback form buy, and why solve it that way here?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Here `remove` equals `add` (XOR is its own inverse), so classic Mo is trivially correct and even faster to code. Rollback is demonstrated to exercise the append-only discipline end-to-end — the shape you *need* when a true `remove` does not exist (the canonical such problem is CF 868F, cited in the ladder). The pedagogical point is that rollback is a window *discipline*, not a specific formula (@sec-mo-p2-interesting, @sec-mo-a2).
:::

**7. [M] In Mo-with-updates the sort key is $(\lfloor\ell/B\rfloor, \lfloor r/B\rfloor, t)$ with $B=n^{2/3}$. Sketch why three pointers land the optimum there.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are $(n/B)^2$ cells of $(\ell,r)$-blocks, and within a cell $t$ advances monotonically $O(m)$ times, so the $t$-movement is $O(m\,n^2/B^2)$. The other two terms are $\ell$-jitter $O(qB)$ and $r$-sweeps $O(n^2/B)$ (one $O(n)$ sweep per $\ell$-block, over $n/B$ blocks). With $q \sim m \sim n$ the $\ell$ and $t$ terms balance at $B = n^{2/3}$, each $O(n^{5/3})$ while the $r$ term $O(n^{4/3})$ is dominated, giving $O(n^{5/3})$. Using $B = \sqrt n$ instead leaves the $t$ term at $O(mn)$ — $O(n^2)$ when $m \sim n$, measurably worse (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
:::

**8. [M] CF 940F asks for the MEX of the *frequencies* in $[\ell,r]$. Name the two tables the window keeps and the $O(1)$ maintenance.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`freq[v]` (how many times value $v$ is present) and `ftf[c]` (how many values currently have frequency exactly $c$). On add of $v$: `ftf[freq[v]]--; freq[v]++; ftf[freq[v]]++` (guarded at $0$); symmetric on remove. The MEX is the smallest $c\ge 1$ with `ftf[c]==0`, found by a scan from $1$; the number of distinct frequency values present bounds the scan, and the whole answer rides the same three-pointer $(\ell,r,t)$ engine (@sec-mo-p3-ml, @sec-mo-a5).
:::

**9. [M] Hilbert order has no clean $O(n\sqrt q)$ proof like block sort. Why still use it, and what did @sec-mo-a4 measure to justify it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Hilbert curve folds $(\ell,r)$ space so consecutive queries stay spatially close, which in practice yields a strictly shorter two-pointer walk than block order (same asymptotics, better constant). @sec-mo-a4 counted total pointer steps on the *same* random query sets under both orderings and asserted `tot_h < tot_b` — the payoff is measured, not just claimed (@sec-mo-a4, @sec-mo-p4-oneocc).
:::

**10. [M] CF 1000F outputs *any* value occurring exactly once in $[\ell,r]$ (or 0). Give the structure the window maintains and the two crossings it must handle.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A `freq[v]` table plus a set `ones` of values currently at frequency exactly 1. Every `add`/`remove` nudges `freq[v]` by $\pm1$; the crossings that matter are $1\to 2$ (value leaves `ones`) and $2\to 1$ (value enters `ones`) — the code tests the count *before* and *after* the nudge. The answer is any element of `ones` (or 0 if empty). Coordinate-compress the values and print `ans[id]` (@sec-mo-p4-oneocc).
:::

**11. [M] The `ftf` table answers mode and exact-$k$ with the same window. Read off: (a) the largest frequency present, (b) how many values appear exactly twice.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) The mode is the largest index $f$ with `ftf[f] > 0`; with a running-mode pointer it drops by at most one when `ftf[mode]` hits $0$, so it stays $O(1)$ amortised. (b) Exactly `ftf[2]` — the count of values whose current frequency is 2. Both read the *same* table, one by scanning its top, the other by direct index (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5-mode).
:::

**12. [M] In the "every value appears exactly thrice" decision, one counter `off` replaces a full table. Define it and the two-transition test.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`off` = number of *present* values whose frequency is not 3. A value is "bad" when $0 < f \ne 3$. Each `add`/`remove` changes one value's count by one: subtract its badness before the nudge, add its badness after. The window is good iff `off == 0`. `bad(0)` is false, so a value leaving the window entirely stops counting immediately (@sec-mo-p5-threeocc).
:::

**13. [H] Prove the two-pointer total is $O(n\sqrt q)$ for block order, bounding $\ell$-movement and $r$-movement separately.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Order by $(\lfloor\ell/B\rfloor, r)$. **$\ell$:** within a block $\ell$ moves $\le B$ per query, and $\ell$-blocks are traversed in $O(B)$ to jump between, so $O(qB)$. **$r$:** inside one $\ell$-block the queries are sorted by $r$, so $r$ sweeps the array at most once, $O(n)$, and there are $n/B$ blocks: $O(n^2/B)$. Sum $= qB + n^2/B$, minimised at $B = n/\sqrt q$ for $O(n\sqrt q)$ (@sec-mo-a1).
:::

**14. [H] Three no-update range queries: CF 86D ($\sum f^2\cdot x$), CF 1000F (single-occurrence witness), and "count values with $f\ge 2$". Which collapse to one window payload and which need a value structure?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
86D and "count $f\ge 2$" are both scalar-accumulator windows: the first keeps a running sum updated by $(2f+1)x$, the second keeps a counter bumped only on the $1\to2$ crossing. CF 1000F is *not* a single scalar — the answer is a value, so it needs a maintained witness set alongside `freq`. All three share the exact same block order and offline `ans[id]`; only the payload grows (@sec-mo-p1-powerful, @sec-mo-p4-oneocc, @sec-mo-a5).
:::

**15. [H] You are handed a problem with $2\cdot 10^5$ queries and heavy point updates that *interleave* and are needed online. Explain why Mo (with or without a time pointer) is the wrong tool and name the right one.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Mo-with-updates assumes updates are *few* and known up front (the $t$ pointer sorts them offline); $q$ genuine online updates make $m\sim q$, blowing the $O(n^{5/3})$ balance and, worse, the answers may be needed between updates so reordering is illegal. A segment tree or Fenwick answers each updated range in $O(\log n)$ online — the honest structure (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-seg, @sec-sqrt-a6).
:::

**16. [H] Rollback restores a snapshot. Show precisely why you must restore *both* the running scalar and the `freq`/`ftf` table, and what a partial restore breaks.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The fringe `add`s mutate the scalar aggregate *and* the tables they read. Rollback pops the dirty `freq` cells and resets the scalar to the snapshot height. Restoring only the scalar leaves `freq` (and any `ftf`) inflated, so the *next* query's `add` starts from a wrong base and its crossings ($0\to1$, $1\to2$) fire incorrectly; restoring only `freq` leaves the scalar over-counted. The two must be rolled back together or every subsequent answer in the block is poisoned (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2-interesting).
:::

## Interview questions

**1. State Mo's algorithm in one sentence and name the single property of the input it exploits.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Mo answers a *batch* of offline range queries by sorting them so consecutive windows overlap heavily, then sliding one $[\ell,r]$ pointer pair with $O(1)$ add/remove. The exploited property is **reorderability**: because no query depends on another's answer, you may permute them and merely remember the original indices (@sec-mo-a1).
:::

**2. Why $B = n/\sqrt q$ and not $\sqrt n$? Give the movement formula you are minimising.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Total pointer travel is $qB$ ($\ell$-jitter) $+\ n^2/B$ ($r$-sweeps across the $n/B$ blocks). AM–GM / calculus minimises it at $B = n/\sqrt q$, yielding $O(n\sqrt q)$. $\sqrt n$ is only optimal when $q\sim n$; for sparse queries it is off by a real, measurable factor (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-pit).
:::

**3. What makes a problem Mo-*legal* versus merely Mo-*fast*? Give a counterexample where Mo is illegal.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Legal = offline (queries known up front, no answer-chaining) plus an $O(1)$ slide. Illegal = adaptive queries: e.g. CF 455D-style inputs where $\ell,r$ are XOR-ed with `lastans`, so you cannot know query $i$ until you answered query $i-1$ — reordering is void and you need an online structure (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-sqrt-a6).
:::

**4. Explain rollback Mo and the situation that forces it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
When you can extend the window in $O(1)$ but cannot cheaply *un*-extend it, sort by $\ell$-block and keep $r$ monotone-forward within the group; per query snapshot the aggregate, `add` the $\le B$ left fringe, read, restore. Amortised $O(n\sqrt n)$ with zero deletes. The canonical forcing problem is CF 868F (cost of a window depends on equal-pairs, no clean remove) (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2).
:::

**5. Mo-with-updates: what is the third pointer, and what discipline does moving it impose?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`t` = how many of the updates have been applied; a query is $(\ell,r,t)$ and you sort by $(\ell/B, r/B, t)$ with $B=n^{2/3}$. Advancing $t$ applies one update and **must stash the cell's old value before overwriting** so retreating $t$ can revert it; if the changed position is inside the window you also remove-old/add-new in the aggregates (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
:::

**6. What does the Hilbert curve buy over block order, and what does it cost you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A shorter practical two-pointer walk: space-filling-curve ordering keeps spatially-near queries near in sort order, so pointers travel fewer steps (better constant, same $O(n\sqrt q)$ family). The cost is losing the clean textbook bound and a uglier key — a recursive `hilbertOrder(x,y,pow,rot)` whose `pow` must cover the grid and whose result must be 64-bit (@sec-mo-a4, @sec-mo-p4).
:::

**7. A query answer is not one number but a *function of the frequency multiset* (mode, exact-$k$, MEX-of-frequencies). How do you keep it $O(1)$ per slide?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Maintain `freq[v]` *and* `ftf[c]` = how many values currently have count $c$, updated together on every add/remove. exact-$k$ is `ftf[k]`; the mode is the top index with `ftf>0` (a running pointer that only drops when `ftf[mode]==0`); MEX-of-frequencies is the smallest $c\ge1$ with `ftf[c]==0`. One leaner trick handles a yes/no shape: a single `off` counter for "all present values at count 3" (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5-mode, @sec-mo-p5-threeocc).
:::

**8. When you would reach for Mo, when for a segment tree, when for sqrt blocks?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Mo: many offline queries, no/few updates, $O(1)$ slide of a non-associative aggregate. Segment tree / Fenwick: online or heavily-updated ranges with an associative $O(\log n)$ combine. Sqrt blocks: online middle ground, $O(\sqrt n)$ per op, no reordering, arbitrary per-block summaries. The gate is reordering freedom — no it means not-Mo (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-sqrt-a6).
:::

**9. Why is tree-path Mo out of scope in a flat-array chapter, and how would you adapt the window to a tree?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The core method is identical but the array is a stand-in for an Euler/first-occurrence tour; path queries become range queries over that tour with a *toggle* (an in/out-of-path flag) so a node counts only while on the current path. That extra machinery (Euler tour + Mo on a subtree vs a path) belongs with tree data structures, so this chapter cites CF 375D / 246E / 600E as the deferred variant rather than solving them (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-mo-pit).
:::

**10. Walk CF 617E: what is the window actually over, and why does the $O(1)$ update count pairs?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The window is over prefix-xor indices $[\ell-1, r]$. A subarray in the original range has xor $k$ iff two prefix values differ by $k$. Adding prefix index $j$ to the window pairs it with every present prefix equal to $p_j\oplus k$, which is `freq[p[j]^k]` — so the pair count rises by that and `freq[p[j]]` is bumped. Removing mirrors it (@sec-mo-p1-xorfav).
:::

**11. What is the single most common Mo bug and how do you catch it in development?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An `add`/`remove` that is not the exact inverse of the other — usually a value structure (`ftf`, a witness set, `off`) updated on add but not symmetrically on remove. The catch is the same as always in this book: keep a raw brute-force oracle (a `Counter`/slice scan) and, after every random query on random data, assert the window answer equals it (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-pit).
:::

**12. Design: $n\le 10^5$ static array, $q\le 10^5$ queries, each asks "is there a value appearing exactly once in $[\ell,r]$ and print one". Give complexity and the structures.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Classic Mo with a `freq` table and a `ones` set maintained across the $1\rightleftarrows2$ crossings; answers are offline so print in input order. $O(n\sqrt q)$ (or Hilbert for the same order with a smaller constant), space $O(n)$. This is CF 1000F; its sibling "*how many* appear once" is `ftf[1]` (@sec-mo-p4-oneocc, @sec-mo-a5).
:::

**13. A colleague set the Mo block size to $\sqrt n$ "because Mo is a sqrt-decomposition algorithm". Correct them precisely.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Classic Mo minimises $qB + n^2/B$, whose optimum is $n/\sqrt q$, not $\sqrt n$; $\sqrt n$ is only right when $q\sim n$. Rollback Mo genuinely uses $\sqrt n$ (its cost is $n^2/B + qB$ with a different balance), and Mo-with-updates uses $n^{2/3}$. Each variant has its own $B$ — copying one across the others is the classic slow-Mo bug (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-pit).
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Classic Mo.** Sort by $(\lfloor\ell/B\rfloor, r)$ with $B = n/\sqrt q$; four widen/narrow loops with $O(1)$ `add`/`remove`; write `ans[id]`; total movement $O(n\sqrt q)$ (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1).
- **Rollback Mo.** When only `add` is cheap: monotone $r$ per left-block, snapshot the aggregate + stack height, add the $\le B$ fringe, read, restore *both* scalar and table; $O(n\sqrt n)$, no deletes (@sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-p2).
- **Mo with updates.** A third, time pointer; sort by $(\ell/B, r/B, t)$ with $B = n^{2/3}$; `apply_time` stashes the old value before overwriting and guards the window touch on `cl <= pos <= cr`; $O(n^{5/3})$ (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3).
- **Hilbert order.** Same window, a different sort key: `hilbertOrder(\ell, r)` (64-bit, `pow` covering the grid); shorter walk in practice, no tidy proof (@sec-mo-a4, @sec-mo-p4).
- **Mo + a value structure.** Hang `ftf[f]` (or a witness set, or an `off` counter) off `freq[v]` and update *everything* in lockstep so mode / exact-$k$ / MEX / "all $=3$" read in $O(1)$ (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5).
- **The triage.** Offline + $O(1)$ slide + no associative combine → Mo; online or answer-chained → segtree / sqrt blocks; tree paths → tree Mo (deferred) (@sec-mo-a6).
:::

- Mo is not a data structure; it is an *ordering* of queries plus one sliding window. Everything else — the block size, the third pointer, the Hilbert key, the value table — is a consequence of what the answer needs when the window nudges by one cell (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-p1..p5).
- The block size is a calculus exercise, not folklore: read the movement cost off the pointers you actually move. $n/\sqrt q$ for two pointers, $\sqrt n$ for rollback, $n^{2/3}$ for three (@sec-mo-a1, @sec-mo-a2, @sec-mo-a3).
- The offline reorder is a *permission you can lose*. `lastans`-chained queries or heavy online updates make Mo illegal, and no amount of clever sorting fixes a wrong-algorithm bug (@sec-mo-a6, @sec-mo-pit).
- The stash is the whole of Mo-with-updates: an update that overwrites without saving is irreversible, so `revert_time` needs the old value you refused to keep (@sec-mo-a3, @sec-mo-p3-ml).
- A value structure turns "how many" into "what shape": `freq`→`ftf` upgrades the window from a scalar to a histogram of counts, and it is the same skeleton with two tables in lockstep (@sec-mo-a5, @sec-mo-p5-mode).
- Hilbert buys a constant, not an exponent; reach for it when $n,q$ are large and the block walk is measurably the bottleneck — and verify it with a movement counter, not a vibe (@sec-mo-a4, @sec-mo-p4-oneocc).
- Every window here is only as trustworthy as its brute-force oracle: stress the exact `add`/`remove` inverses, the restore-everything in rollback, and the stash in the time pointer, after every random operation (@sec-mo-pit).

## Practice ladder

Ordered by pattern. The problems solved in Part B are marked `.solved`; self-authored solved tasks are named with their section anchor and are fully stressed against a brute force in this chapter. Every other entry is "solve it after the lesson named"; ratings/names are verbatim from the judge.

::: {.practice}
- [CF 86D · Powerful array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/86/D){.solved rating="2200"} — the canonical classic-Mo warm-up: $\sum f(x)^2\cdot x$, $(2f+1)v$ slide (@sec-mo-p1-powerful)
- [CF 617E · XOR and Favorite Number](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/617/E){.solved rating="2200"} — pair count over a prefix-xor window (@sec-mo-p1-xorfav)
- [CF 703D · Mishka and Interesting sum](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/703/D){.solved rating="2100"} — solved in rollback form to exercise append/snapshot/restore (@sec-mo-p2-interesting)
- Distinct values per range, by rollback (@sec-mo-p2-distinct) — self-authored: the rollback skeleton with the simplest payload, brute + stress
- [CF 940F · Machine Learning](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/940/F){.solved rating="2600"} — Mo-with-updates flagship; MEX of frequencies, the stash discipline (@sec-mo-p3-ml)
- Distinct values per range with point updates (@sec-mo-p3-distinct) — self-authored: the three-pointer engine verbatim, a plain distinct payload, brute + stress
- [CF 1000F · One Occurrence](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1000/F){.solved rating="2400"} — single-occurrence witness by Hilbert order (@sec-mo-p4-oneocc)
- Distinct count by Hilbert order (@sec-mo-p4-distinct) — self-authored: Hilbert as a drop-in key, asserted equal to block order and the brute
- Range mode (largest frequency) (@sec-mo-p5-mode) — self-authored: `freq`+`ftf` with a running-mode pointer, brute + stress
- Every value exactly thrice (@sec-mo-p5-threeocc) — self-authored: a single `off` counter decision, brute + stress
- [CF 868F · Yet Another Minimization Problem](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/868/F){rating="2500"} — the judge problem where rollback is the standard solution (equal-pair cost, no clean remove); @sec-mo-a2
- [SPOJ DQUERY · Distinct Queries](https://www.spoj.com/problems/DQUERY/){difficulty="Medium"} — the classic no-update "count distinct in range" that Mo trivialises; a first solo window (@sec-mo-a1)
- [CSES 2416 · Distinct Values Queries](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/2416){difficulty="Hard"} — #distinct offline; try Mo, then compare the persistent/Fenwick online answer (@sec-mo-a6)
- [CF 375D · Tree and Queries](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/375/D){rating="2400"} — *tree-path* Mo (Euler tour + toggle); cited as the deferred variant, not solved in a flat-array chapter (@sec-mo-a6)
- [CF 246E · Blood Cousins Return](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/246/E){rating="2400"} — subtree-distinct by the same deferred tree-Mo technique (@sec-mo-a6)
- [CF 600E · Lomsat gelral](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/600/E){rating="2300"} — subtree mode; solvable by DSU-on-tree or tree-Mo, the value-structure idea of @sec-mo-p5 on a tree (@sec-mo-a5)
:::

## Further reading

- [CP-Algorithms — Mo's algorithm](https://cp-algorithms.com/misc/mo-algorithm.html) — the block reordering, the $O(n\sqrt q)$ bound, and the $B = n/\sqrt q$ sizing of @sec-mo-a1 worked through in C++.
- [CP-Algorithms — Mo's algorithm with updates](https://cp-algorithms.com/misc/mo-with-updates.html) — the third, time pointer and the $n^{2/3}$ block size behind @sec-mo-a3 and @sec-mo-p3-ml.
- [CP-Algorithms — Mo's algorithm on trees](https://cp-algorithms.com/misc/mo-on-trees.html) — the deferred tree-path/subtree variant cited at @sec-mo-a6 (CF 375D, 246E, 600E); the home of this method in the trees volume.
- [E-maxx (ru) — Mo's algorithm and Hilbert-curve ordering](https://cp-algorithms.com/) and the kactl `hilbertOrder` reference — the space-filling-curve key of @sec-mo-a4 and @sec-mo-p4, including the `pow`/`rot` recursion.
- [SPOJ DQUERY](https://www.spoj.com/problems/DQUERY/) — the canonical #distinct warm-up that every Mo textbook opens with (@sec-mo-a1).
- [CPH — Chapter 10 (Advanced Data Structures)](https://cses.fi/book/book.pdf) — the offline-range-query family that frames Mo against persistent structures (@sec-mo-a6).
